Nigeria ready to host 126 countries at 2026 PR forum
items.description: By Chidinma Chukwu, Abuja The Federal Government has declared its readiness to host the 2026 World Public Relations Forum (WPRF), with representatives from more than 126 countries and leading international institutions expected at the global event scheduled to hold in Abuja from November 15 to 22. The Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, gave the assurance at a world press conference in Abuja on Wednesday. The forum, to be hosted under the leadership of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu as Chief Host, is expected to bring together global public relations experts, communication professionals, policymakers and representatives of major international organisations to discuss the future of responsible communication. Speaking at the event, Idris described Nigeria’s selection as host as significant recognition of the country’s growing influence in global communication and public relations. He appreciated the Global Alliance for Public Relations and Communication Management and the African Public Relations Association (APRA) for entrusting Nigeria with the responsibility of hosting the international and continental gatherings simultaneously. The minister noted that Nigeria would become the first country in West Africa and the second in Africa to host the World Public Relations Forum, describing the opportunity as a major milestone for the country and the continent. According to him, the forum would provide Nigeria with an important platform to showcase its institutional capacity, strengthen international partnerships and contribute to conversations shaping the global communication industry. With the theme, “Responsible Communication: The Voice of the World,” the 2026 forum is expected to address critical challenges confronting the communication industry, particularly the growing influence of digital platforms, artificial intelligence and emerging technologies. Idris warned that the rapid transformation of the information environment had heightened concerns over misinformation, disinformation and the erosion of public trust. He stressed that communication professionals must remain committed to truth, accuracy, transparency and ethical conduct. The minister maintained that the responsibility of public relations practitioners should extend beyond protecting institutional reputations and promoting organisational interests to safeguarding the public interest and ensuring that citizens have access to credible information. He also highlighted the Federal Government’s support for the establishment of the UNESCO Category 2 International Media and Information Literacy Institute (IMILI) in Abuja. He described the initiative as a strategic investment in building an informed society, particularly among young people, by equipping citizens with the knowledge and skills to identify misleading information and navigate the increasingly complex digital environment. On government communication, Idris emphasised the need for a more inclusive and transparent approach, saying effective communication must involve listening to citizens, addressing their concerns and providing reliable information to support informed decision-making. He said the Federal Ministry of Information and National Orientation was working closely with the Nigerian Institute of Public Relations (NIPR) and other relevant institutions to ensure adequate arrangements for protocol, security, logistics, hospitality and stakeholder engagement ahead of the forum. The minister assured international delegates of Nigeria’s hospitality and encouraged participants to explore the country’s cultural heritage, economic opportunities and tourism potential during their visit. Earlier, the President of NIPR, Dr Ike Neliaku, commended Idris for his support and commitment throughout Nigeria’s campaign to secure the hosting rights and preparations for the international event. Similarly, the Secretary-General of APRA, Dr Omoniyi Ibietan, described Nigeria’s hosting of the WPRF alongside the 37th APRA Conference as a historic opportunity for Africa to strengthen its collective voice and influence the direction of global communication. He stressed the importance of greater continental collaboration, noting that the gathering would enable African communication professionals to speak with one voice on issues affecting the industry and the wider society. Also speaking, the President and Chief Executive Officer of the Global Alliance for Public Relations and Communication Management, Professor Justin Green, disclosed that more than 126 countries were expected at the forum. He added that representatives of the United Nations, World Bank, African Union and European Commission would also participate, underscoring the international significance of the gathering. Green commended President Tinubu and Idris for their support, describing the minister’s commitment as instrumental to Nigeria’s successful bid to host the event. The post Nigeria ready to host 126 countries at 2026 PR forum appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: GAIA, GAYO, Experts call for Zero Waste Solutions at COP31
items.description: Climate advocates, researchers, youth leaders and local government officials have urged governments and climate financiers at COP31 to reject waste incineration and put their money into waste prevention, reuse, repair and composting instead. At a press conference titled “Zero Waste COP – Incinerators Out. Zero Waste In.”, organised by the Global Alliance for Incinerator Alternatives (GAIA) on 11 November, speakers said the climate impact of waste can only be cut by tackling it at the source, not by building more facilities to burn or bury it. “Zero waste is climate action, but only when we address the problem at its source. We cannot solve the waste crisis by building more infrastructure to burn or dispose of what we produce,” said Mariel Vilella, Climate Program Director at GAIA. “Preventing waste, expanding reuse and composting organic materials are practical and proven solutions that can cut emissions while delivering benefits for communities.” Rotting rubbish is a major source of methane, a gas about 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide at trapping heat over 20 years. According to the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC), municipal solid waste and wastewater are the third-largest and fastest-growing source of human-caused methane, at nearly 20 per cent (about one in every five tonnes). Without action, these emissions are projected to rise by 6 to 18 per cent between 2020 and 2030. The CCAC also estimates that about 40 per cent of the world’s waste is openly burned (two in every five bags of rubbish), releasing black carbon and other harmful pollutants. Around 2.5 billion people (about three in every ten people on Earth) lack adequate waste management services, mainly because city authorities cannot afford them. Methane in the atmosphere reached a record 1,948 parts per billion in 2025, according to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). UNEP’s Emissions Gap Report 2026 says global methane emissions must fall by at least 25 per cent (one-quarter) by 2035, compared with 2025. For organic waste, the CCAC says methane must fall by at least 30 to 35 per cent (about one-third) to keep the 1.5°C goal within reach. The warming is already here. WMO’s State of the Climate update, released at the start of COP31, puts the global average temperature for January to September 2026 at 1.47°C above pre-industrial levels, with 2015–2026 set to be the 12 warmest years on record. UNEP says current policies put the world on course for about 2.8°C of warming by 2100 (nearly double the 1.5°C limit). Speakers warned that the climate problem with waste begins long before disposal. Plastic production is closely tied to fossil fuels, with emissions across its lifecycle. “We cannot tackle climate change while allowing plastic production to keep expanding. Reducing plastic production and scaling reuse must be part of any credible climate strategy,” said Mohamed Kamal, Coordinator of Climate Action Network Arab World (CANAW). A new GAIA report, Africa’s Waste Crisis Is Attracting the Wrong Solution: Waste-to-Energy Incineration , released on 15 October, examines 15 waste-to-energy projects and proposals across 10 African countries: Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Morocco, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, South Africa, Uganda and Zimbabwe. Only one, the Reppie plant in Ethiopia, is operating. Two are under construction and twelve are at the approval, financing, planning or proposal stage. Together, they carry more than US$4 billion in capital costs for an estimated 520–550 MW of capacity. The report finds that African public funds are the largest source of finance for these projects, and that long contracts can shift economic risk onto the public even when projects are described as private. Near Ethiopia’s Koshe dumpsite, interviews found a 50 per cent drop (half) in waste pickers’ earnings linked to the Reppie incinerator. GAIA says most of Africa’s waste is organic and wet, so it burns poorly and may need fossil fuel support. Incinerators also release toxic pollutants and ash, cost hundreds of millions of dollars, and lock cities into 25–30 year contracts that require a constant supply of waste. The CCAC notes that more than half of municipal solid waste in developing countries is organic. The report calls for a moratorium on new incineration agreements until independent assessments are done, public disclosure of contracts and impact assessments, formal integration of waste pickers, and investment in source separation, collection, composting and recycling. “Incineration can lock municipalities into costly infrastructure, expose communities to harmful pollution, and divert resources from more inclusive zero waste alternatives,” said Weyinmi Okotie, Executive Director of Green Knowledge Foundation. “Africa needs solutions that respond to its actual waste realities, not expensive technologies that create new problems.” Speakers said the financing imbalance is a major barrier to the zero waste transition. “Governments and climate financiers must correct this imbalance and make climate finance accessible to the communities and cities already delivering solutions,” said Jacob Johnson Attakpah, Zero Waste Director of the Green Africa Youth Organisation (GAYO). The scale of the need is large. Countries that have costed their national climate plans report finance needs of about US$3.6 trillion, including US$893–898 billion for adaptation, according to the UN Climate Change secretariat’s 2026 synthesis of national climate plans. That synthesis also found that 89 per cent of countries report measures to cut methane from waste. Yet money for cleaner air remains thin: the Clean Air Fund’s State of Global Air Quality Funding 2026 found that funding aimed directly at outdoor air pollution is still less than 1 per cent of international development funding (less than US$1 in every US$100), and 89 per cent of air quality funding between 2020 and 2024 came as loans. The returns are high. UNEP and the CCAC’s Hidden Assets report, published in September, found that every US$1 invested in 25 measures that tackle air pollution and climate change together, including clean cooking, brings back about US$15 in economic benefits. The measures could prevent about 144 million premature deaths by 2050 and avoid about 0.34°C of warming by mid-century. Cities are central to the solution, said Shahriar Hossain of the Government of Bangladesh. He said cities are on the frontlines of the waste and climate crises but are also where many of the solutions can happen, and that they need strong political support, consistent public investment and policies that make zero waste systems possible at scale. Attakpah, who leads GAYO’s delegation at COP31, said the group is among the African organisations pressing for finance to reach community-led waste solutions. “The litmus test of climate finance is whether it reaches the people and services capable of delivering change and results; that means financing the daily work of separation, collection, reuse and composting while recognizing the people who make it possible, waste pickers and other actors in the informal sector,” he said. The Ghana-based organisation won the 2024 Earthshot Prize in the “Clean our air” category, worth £1 million, for its Zero Waste Accra model, after being nominated by the Clean Air Fund. The project diverts organic, plastic and electronic waste from landfills and open burning, supports 500 waste pickers and informal collectors, and aims to divert 4,000 tonnes of waste by 2030 while cutting greenhouse gas and particulate emissions by 70 per cent compared with open burning, according to the Clean Air Fund. In July 2026, the City of Accra launched a LOW-Methane Portfolio, developed with technical support from GAYO, GAIA and C40 Cities. It aims to cut methane from waste disposal by at least 30 per cent by 2030, separate at least half of the city’s organic waste at source by 2030, and reduce methane emissions by about 13,500 tonnes a year by 2040. At national level, Ghana’s updated Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), its climate plan for 2025–2035, were presented for validation in Accra in May. The plan is expected to cost about US$53.3 billion over ten years (about US$5.3 billion a year), and circular economy and waste management is one of its five pillars, with measures including recycling, biodigesters and methane capture. END.

items.title: Huelga general 11N y actualidad política, en directo | Miles de personas recorren las calles de numerosas ciudades en las manifestaciones de la huelga general
items.description: Miles de personas recorren ya las calles de numerosas ciudades de España como colofón a la jornada de huelga general de este 11-N, la primera en 14 años. Las marchas más multitudinarias son las de Madrid y Barcelona, con decenas de miles de manifestantes en cada una de ellas que corean lemas a favor del acceso a la vivienda y de la subida de salarios y contra la especulación. Los sindicatos mayoritarios UGT y CC OO han augurado que las marchas van a ser “masivas” pese a la lluvia y han celebrado la jornada de huelga como “muy exitosa”, con seguimiento “por encima de lo esperado”, mientras que las patronales han tachado de “bajo” el seguimiento. Se han producido algunos incidentes en piquetes y protestas que se han saldado con al menos 42 detenidos en varias ciudades. La jornada ha arrancado con cortes de carreteras en Madrid, Valencia, Barcelona y otras ciudades y el transporte en general se ha visto afectado, con la cancelación del 24% de los AVE o el 10% de los Cercanías y de más de 280 vuelos programados. En Cataluña, la huelga dejará sin transporte público a los residentes durante 10 horas. Además, una manifestación ha cortado la Gran Vía y ha provocado el cierre de comercios. Se han vivido momentos de tensión en esta marcha cuando la policía ha intentado dispersar a los manifestantes. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Egyptian journalist’s retrial adjourned as UN warns of ‘assaults on press freedom’
items.description: A criminal court in Cairo has postponed the retrial of the prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, whose case has drawn international condemnation. Wednesday’s opening hearing was adjourned until 18 November after defence lawyers representing the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr requested a new judge. The UN has warned of “widening assaults on press freedom by Egyptian authorities, including the targeting, persecution and harassment of independent journalists”. Attalah told the BBC that a recent crackdown was meant to “send a chilling message” to “the very few newsrooms that are left”. She warned: “Everybody should be careful, everybody should be scared, everybody should be wondering if they are next.” Set up 13 years ago, Mada Masr became Egypt’s leading independent news site with Attalah as its editor-in-chief and co-founder. Last month, the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court convicted her of running a website without a licence – which she said she had tried in vain for years to obtain. She was issued a hefty fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds ($56,000; £42,000) and Mada Masr was ordered to shut down. After that trial, Attalah found that a court had previously given her a one-year prison sentence, without her knowledge, for “spreading false news” – a charge often used against journalists and dissidents – as well as operating a website without a licence. It was issued in absentia in 2024, even though she was in the country at the time. Attalah is now being retried in that case by the same judge. At the opening session, Attalah’s defence team requested the judge’s recusal, arguing that he had “already formed a conviction in mind against the defendant”, Mada Masr cited its lawyer Hassan al-Azhar as saying. The judge went into recess before adjourning proceedings for a week to allow the court to consider the defence’s request, he added. Mada Masr also said Attalah’s appeal against last month’s conviction was scheduled to take place on 25 November. Egypt has largely stifled freedom of the press, ranking 169th out of 180 countries for press freedom, according to Reporters Without Borders’ 2026 analysis. The group says that at least 26 journalists who were arrested in recent years remain in detention. While most newspapers and television stations now keep to government lines, Mada Masr remained a rare, independent and investigative news source in Egypt. However, since 2017 the site could only be viewed from outside the country. It had reported on alleged corruption and human rights abuses, and provided deep coverage of politics and economics, as well as regional upheaval and wars in Libya, Sudan and Gaza. In her BBC interview on Sunday, Attalah insisted that the factual reporting and professional standards of Mada Masr had an important role to play in Egyptian society, which could benefit the government. “It’s much better if you have a little space left to have it open for professional media organisations who do rigorous reporting, because if we disappear, then you make the space for conspiracies and disinformation,” she said. “People need to know, people need to consume information and you’re shooting yourself in the foot if you’re killing the newsrooms that do it properly.” In September, six journalists with the independent fact-checking platform, Matsda2sh – constituting its entire newsroom – were arrested in home raids by the Egyptian authorities and held incommunicado for nearly a week. They have since been charged with joining the Muslim Brotherhood and financing terrorism, and their lawyers report that several were beaten and electrocuted in detention. They say that no evidence has been presented linking them to the Brotherhood. Egypt’s former president Mohammed Morsi – who was backed by the Muslim Brotherhood – was removed from power by the military, led by Abdul Fattah al-Sisi, in July 2013 after widespread protests. Under Sisi, who became president the following year, the Islamist movement was classed as a terrorist organisation, leading to a widespread clampdown. On Tuesday, a spokesperson for the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Thameen Al-Kheetan, called for the Matsda2sh reporters to be released, with all charges dropped. He also said the case against Attalah “raises fresh concerns regarding due process and fair trial”. “We call on Egypt to end all forms of harassment of journalists and media outlets, and to respect and fulfil the right to freedom of expression, including the right to information,” Al-Kheetan said. “The steps taken to suppress the continued work of both Matsda2sh and Mada Masr must be overturned. The people of Egypt have a right to read and hear views expressed through these fora on issues of legitimate public concern.” Attalah has suggested the authorities might again be trying to silence independent voices at a time of economic strain in Egypt and regional instability. It has been widely noted that recent legal action against journalists comes after the US State Department waived human rights conditions on $320m (£240m) in its foreign military funding for Egypt in September. This allowed the funds to be released as part of Washington’s annual $1.3bn military aid package. The BBC asked US Secretary of State Marco Rubio whether he had raised the recent crackdown on independent journalism with Egypt’s Foreign Minister, Badr Abdelatty, at their meeting about regional tensions in Paris on Monday. “We didn’t discuss it today,” Rubio said. “But… like anything else in foreign policy, there’s always a balancing act to further the national interest of the United States. And in the end, Egypt has been a reliable and good defence partner of the United States.” “That doesn’t mean you agree with everything another government does,” he went on, adding that he was not “opining about their journalists”.

items.title: Eswatini gives illegal foreign businesses 12 months to leave
items.description: Businesses owned by Asian nationals are being closed across Eswatini, previously known as Swaziland, as the government cracks down on foreign-owned enterprises. It follows parliament’s approval of a law that seeks to increase ownership and participation by emaSwati, as citizens of the kingdom are known. The legislation comes after complaints from local traders that foreign-owned businesses are encroaching on traditional retail markets, increasing competition and threatening livelihoods. South Africa has witnessed more severe enforcement action, including raids, arrests and the disruption of foreign-run informal businesses, while Kenya has also stepped up action against foreign traders. Eswatini is a small landlocked kingdom in southern Africa, led by absolute monarch King Mswati III, where about 70% of its population live below the poverty line. Those angered by economic hardships have become increasingly vocal in demanding political reform. Pro-democracy protests broke out in 2021- and the royal family has faced criticism by activists for its extravagant spending as many emaSwati with a job work in neighbouring South Africa and send their earnings home. The government says the new law is intended to expand economic opportunities, amid concerns that poverty and hunger could fuel further political unrest. But the implementation of the Citizen Economic Empowerment Act has sparked a heated debate in Eswatini’s parliament, with MPs divided over how quickly foreign businesses owners should be required to leave. On Tuesday, Mbabane East MP Welcome Dlamini said that officials from the trade ministry had already begun enforcing the law by closing Asian-owned shops. Hhohho Regional MP Tanele Magagula called for immediate action, saying: “Businesses owned by foreigners in the rural areas must be seized immediately.” Dlamini questioned whether local entrepreneurs were ready to take over the businesses, arguing that foreigners should be given time to train their successors. “Why can’t we give the Asians or foreigners at least three years before ‘kicking them’ out so that emaSwati can learn to run the businesses?” he asked. Magagula rejected the suggestion, questioning why struggling local traders should have to wait while struggling economically. “Why must we wait for three years while emaSwati suffer?” she asked. Parliament subsequently agreed that foreign business owners should be given at least 12 months to leave. However, unless the law is formally amended to reflect that timeline, the ministry could continue enforcing its provisions. The closures follow inspections launched by the trade ministry in August. Some businesses inspected in areas such as the capital, Mbabane, were found to be fully compliant. Nonetheless the inspections also raised concerns about working conditions and administrative practices at foreign-owned enterprises, including complaints by employees over days off, annual leave and overtime. At least one case remains under investigation. The crackdown comes amid growing pressure on foreign-owned businesses elsewhere in the region, particularly in South Africa, which has experienced repeated outbreaks of xenophobic violence, often targeting African migrants. Anti-migrant groups there set 30 June as a deadline for undocumented migrants to leave the country – and their campaigns this year has often been accompanied by violence and attacks on foreign-owned businesses. Two Ghanaian and two Nigerian nationals were reported killed amid the tensions. Kenya has also stepped up enforcement against foreign traders, bringing renewed attention to the treatment of foreign nationals and their businesses across the region.

items.title: Indonesia’s vice president resigns over high school certificate that was ruled invalid
items.description: Indonesia’s Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power. Gibran’s resignation comes after Indonesia’s Supreme Court ruled that a high-school certificate used during Gibran’s 2024 election campaign was invalid. The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran. It is not clear if Prabowo has formally accepted the resignation. Gibran is the eldest son of former President Joko Widodo, known as Jokowi, who supported his former rival Prabowo in the 2024 election. Prabowo won, but the two men have since drifted apart.

items.title: JOJ Dakar 2026 : Ameth Diop décroche le bronze en Taekwondo
items.description: Le Sénégalais Ameth Diop a remporté la médaille de bronze en taekwondo, dans la catégorie des moins de 73 kg, aux Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026. Le combattant sénégalais s'est arrêté aux portes de la finale après sa défaite en demi-finale face à un adversaire azerbaïdjanais, mercredi 11 novembre. Avant cette confrontation, Ameth Diop avait réalisé une belle performance en quart de finale. Opposé au Saoudien Fawaz Almasaari, il s'était imposé en deux rounds (12-9 et 22-18), soit un succès 2-0, pour valider sa qualification en demi-finale. Cette victoire lui avait déjà assuré une place sur le podium, avec au minimum une médaille de bronze. Malgré son revers dans le dernier carré, le Sénégalais repart ainsi avec une distinction aux JOJ disputés à domicile. Cette nouvelle récompense vient enrichir le bilan du taekwondo sénégalais, déjà marqué par le sacre de Marie Sarr chez les moins de 55 kg et la médaille de bronze d'Aïda Touré dans la catégorie des moins de 63 kg. Le Sénégal confirme ainsi sa présence sur les podiums de cette discipline lors de ces Jeux.

items.title: Souveraineté numérique : le président burkinabè lance l’enregistrement massif pour l’identifiant unique
items.description: Le president burkinabe Ibrahim Traore a preside, le 11 novembre a Ouagadougou, le lancement officiel de l'operation d'enregistrement massif de la population au registre national de l'identifiant unique electronique. La ceremonie s'est deroulee en presence de membres du gouvernement, d'autorites coutumieres et religieuses ainsi que de responsables des institutions republicaines. Presentee par les autorites comme une nouvelle etape dans la modernisation de l'administration, cette initiative vise egalement a renforcer la souverainete numerique du Burkina Faso. L'operation s'inscrit dans les efforts engages par le gouvernement pour moderniser l'etat civil et accelerer la transformation numerique des services publics. Elle doit notamment permettre d'ameliorer l'identification des personnes, de fiabiliser les donnees demographiques et de faciliter la planification des politiques publiques. L'aboutissement d'un processus engage depuis une decennie Lors de la ceremonie, Ibrahim Traore a rappele que le lancement de cette operation marquait l'aboutissement d'un processus engage depuis une dizaine d'annees pour doter chaque personne d'un identifiant unique. Selon le chef de l'etat, ce dispositif permettra de mieux connaître l'effectif reel de la population et d'optimiser la planification des depenses dans les differents secteurs sociaux. Pour sa part, la ministre de la Transition digitale, des Postes et des Communications electroniques, Aminata Zerbo-Sabane, a souligne que les donnees collectees seraient hebergees dans des centres de donnees situes au Burkina Faso. La plateforme, developpee par des ingenieurs burkinabe, doit ainsi permettre aux autorites de conserver la maîtrise nationale du systeme d'identification.

items.title: How Do Enterprise Brands Scale TikTok Influencer Marketing?
items.description: Running a TikTok campaign with five creators is manageable. Running campaigns with dozens or hundreds of creators across different products, countries, internal teams, and agencies is a very different challenge. For large brands, the real question is not simply how to find more influencers. It is how to scale TikTok influencer marketing without losing control over creative quality, brand standards, budgets, reporting, and local relevance. That requires systems. Brands need repeatable ways to identify creators, review content, approve campaigns, manage payments, protect the brand, measure results, and learn from previous activity. A specialist TikTok marketing agency can support that process by bringing creator strategy, campaign operations, paid media, and performance measurement into one coordinated structure. The goal is to move from individual creator activations to a repeatable marketing channel. To Scale TikTok Influencer Marketing, Start With the Operating Model Before adding more creators, enterprise brands need to decide how the influencer program will actually operate. Large organizations may have global marketing teams, regional managers, product divisions, legal departments, procurement teams, local agencies, and paid media specialists involved in the same campaign. Without clear ownership, adding more creators can simply add more complexity. Most large influencer programs generally follow one of three models: Centralized: A global team controls strategy, creator selection, budgets, approvals, and reporting. Decentralized: Regional teams manage their own campaigns independently. Hybrid: Central teams establish standards while regional teams control local execution. For multinational brands, the hybrid model can often provide a useful balance. The organization can standardize contracts, reporting, creator-vetting requirements, brand safety, and campaign objectives while allowing regional teams to adapt language, creators, cultural references, and content formats. Vanguard has highlighted the growing importance of having a clear digital strategy rather than simply maintaining a social media presence. Its coverage of why businesses need digital strategy reflects the same principle. Scale should begin with structure, not volume. Standardize What Does Not Need to Change One of the easiest ways for influencer programs to become inefficient is for every campaign to start from zero. Enterprise teams should standardize repeatable processes such as: Creator vetting criteria Campaign brief templates Contract structures Content approval stages Usage rights Disclosure requirements Brand safety checks Reporting definitions Payment processes Performance dashboards This does not mean every campaign should look identical. It means teams should avoid rebuilding the administrative side of the program each time. For example, a US campaign and a South Korean campaign may feature different creators and different creative concepts, but both can still use the same basic approval workflow and reporting framework. That consistency becomes increasingly important as the number of campaigns grows. Build a Creator Portfolio Instead of Relying on a Few Big Names Brands trying to scale TikTok influencer marketing should avoid depending entirely on celebrity or macro creators. Different creator tiers can play different roles. Large creators can provide broad reach. Mid-tier creators can offer a balance between reach and engagement. Micro and niche creators may provide stronger relevance within particular communities or product categories. The right mix depends on the campaign. A major launch may use several high-reach creators supported by a wider group of smaller voices. An always-on customer acquisition program may rely on a larger network of creators producing content continuously. Vanguard’s coverage of Nigeria’s creator economy shows how creators can build audiences that extend well beyond their home markets, which is increasingly important for global brands looking for talent with cross-border reach. The key is to build a portfolio rather than searching for one “perfect” influencer. Make Creator Vetting Repeatable As creator volume grows, suitability becomes more important. Brands need a consistent way to evaluate potential partners. That may include: Audience geography Audience demographics Average and median views Engagement quality Historical content Previous brand partnerships Brand conflicts Audience sentiment Content category Past campaign performance TikTok’s own Creator Suitability Report emphasizes factors such as brand alignment, audience trust, creator authenticity, and safety. At enterprise level, those checks should become part of a standard process. A centralized framework also helps regional teams move faster because they already know which requirements a creator must meet before approval. Create Global Standards but Localize the Creative One of the hardest parts of scaling internationally is finding the right balance between consistency and localization. A global brand usually wants one positioning and one campaign objective. But audiences in London, Los Angeles, Lagos, or Seoul may respond to very different creators, humor, language, trends, and storytelling styles. A practical approach is to divide the brief into two layers. The global layer covers: Campaign objective Core brand message Required product claims Prohibited topics Key brand guidelines Measurement framework The local layer covers: Creator selection Language Cultural references Local trends Posting times Creative execution Vanguard’s coverage of the expanding cross-border creator economy illustrates how digital audiences increasingly extend beyond one country. Global campaigns therefore need enough structure to stay recognizable without becoming so rigid that every market receives the same creative. Build an Always-On Creator Pipeline Brands often struggle when creator sourcing begins only after a campaign is approved. At scale, sourcing should be continuous. Creators can be organized according to: Market Audience Product category Creator tier Content style Historical performance Cost Brand suitability Platform specialization Over time, this creates a useful internal knowledge base. Instead of starting from zero each time, teams can return to creators who have already performed well while continuing to test new talent. Vanguard’s recent interview about the business infrastructure behind creators highlights an important point: creator marketing increasingly depends on systems, technology, and commercial processes that audiences rarely see. That hidden infrastructure becomes even more important at enterprise scale. Use Paid Media to Scale Strong Creator Content Organic reach should not be the only way to expand a successful influencer campaign. When brands want to scale TikTok influencer marketing , paid amplification can extend the reach of creator content that has already demonstrated strong performance. A practical process might look like this: Creators produce multiple concepts. Organic performance identifies stronger videos. Paid media increases the reach of those assets. Performance data then influences the next creator brief. TikTok’s TikTok One platform is designed to help brands and agencies connect creator discovery, creative production, and advertising workflows. This model allows creators to function as both distribution partners and sources of advertising creative. It also reduces the need to guess which content deserves more media spend. Keep Measurement Consistent Across Markets Enterprise programs become difficult to evaluate when every region reports success differently. One team may focus on views. Another may report engagement. Another may prioritize revenue. Those metrics can all be useful, but they need to sit within a common framework. For awareness campaigns, brands might track: Reach Impressions Video views Watch time Engagement Brand lift For consideration: Click-through rate Website sessions Product views Search activity For performance: Conversions Cost per acquisition Revenue Return on ad spend Customer acquisition cost Vanguard has also reported on how platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp have become increasingly important for business operations, customer acquisition, digital advertising, and e-commerce . The larger lesson applies across platforms: social media activity increasingly needs to connect with measurable business outcomes. Use Campaign Data to Improve the Next Campaign To scale TikTok influencer marketing effectively, performance data cannot remain trapped inside individual campaign reports. Brands should build feedback loops. Teams should be able to answer questions such as: Which creator profiles consistently perform well? Which hooks improve watch time? Which products generate stronger creator response? Which markets respond better to educational content? Which creator assets perform well when amplified? Which audiences convert at the lowest cost? These insights gradually turn influencer marketing from experimentation into institutional knowledge. Vanguard’s coverage of digital marketing trends has similarly highlighted TikTok’s role in discovery, short-form storytelling, user-generated content, mobile-first retail behavior, and evolving brand visibility. For enterprise teams, the important part is using those lessons repeatedly rather than treating each campaign as an isolated project. Build Compliance Into the Scaling Process More creators also mean more opportunities for mistakes. Sponsored partnerships need clear disclosure, particularly when campaigns cross markets. In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission says creators should disclose material relationships with brands, including payments, free products, discounts, and other benefits. The FTC’s influencer disclosure guidance says those disclosures should be clear and difficult for viewers to miss. Brands should build compliance requirements into campaign briefs, contracts, approvals, and creator training rather than handling them after publication. International programs may also need local legal review because advertising rules can vary between markets. Do Not Expand Everywhere at Once Enterprise teams sometimes assume that scaling means launching in every major market at the same time. That can multiply problems before the operating model has been tested. A more controlled approach is to establish the system in a smaller number of priority markets. Test the creator selection process. Test contracts. Test approvals. Test paid amplification. Test reporting. Test how global messaging translates locally. Once the process works reliably, expansion becomes easier. The objective is not simply to increase campaign size. The objective is to make the next campaign easier to operate than the previous one. The Goal Is Repeatability The best way to scale TikTok influencer marketing is not to add as many creators as possible. It is to build a system that can handle more creators, more markets, and more campaigns without sacrificing creative quality, brand control, or campaign measurement . That requires standardized processes, local flexibility, consistent creator vetting, strong reporting, paid media integration, and an always-on pipeline of talent. Enterprise influencer marketing becomes truly scalable when each campaign produces knowledge that improves the next one. At that point, TikTok stops being a collection of individual creator partnerships and becomes a repeatable marketing channel that can grow alongside the business. items.title: CAC, EY warn directors against governance failures
items.description: By Peter Egwuatu The Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) has warned company directors against treating regulatory compliance as the sole responsibility of company secretaries, saying weak corporate records and governance failures could undermine business credibility, investment prospects and access to credit. The Registrar-General and Chief Executive Officer of CAC, Hussaini Ishaq Magaji, gave the warning at the 2026 Audit Committee Transformation Summit organised by Ernst & Young (EY) in Lagos on Wednesday. Magaji said directors’ responsibilities extended beyond strategy, profitability and risk management to protecting the integrity of their companies’ legal identities. He noted that outdated corporate records, undisclosed changes in ownership and failure to file annual returns could expose companies to regulatory sanctions, reputational damage and diminished investor confidence. According to him, “Directors must demonstrate diligence, transparency and accountability by ensuring accurate corporate records, timely statutory filings and proper disclosure of persons with significant control. “The era of filing annual returns as an annual ritual is over. The Corporate Affairs Commission is asking Nigerian boards and companies to move beyond merely filing annual returns towards continuous accountability, transparent ownership, accurate records and credible governance.” He added that companies with transparent ownership structures and disciplined governance would be better positioned to attract investments, secure credit, participate in public procurement and pursue business partnerships. Also speaking, Amina Maida, who represented the Executive Vice Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), said effective audit committees were essential to strengthening corporate resilience amid technological changes, cybersecurity threats and evolving regulatory requirements. She said the NCC issued corporate governance guidelines for the communications industry in 2025, outlining board and committee responsibilities, including risk management, internal controls and audit oversight. In his welcome address, EY Regional Managing Partner, West Africa, Anthony Oputa, said audit committees were performing their oversight responsibilities in an increasingly complex environment shaped by evolving regulatory expectations, geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty, technological disruption, sustainability considerations and significant changes in financial reporting. Oputa, who was represented by Jamiu Olakisan, Assurance Leader, EY West Africa, said the developments were placing greater demands on audit committees to strengthen accounting and internal control systems, enhance corporate transparency, safeguard audit quality and reinforce stakeholder confidence. He said audit committees must look beyond traditional compliance and financial reporting by anticipating emerging risks, asking more incisive questions and providing effective oversight of critical issues, including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, sustainability, taxation, talent management and the implementation of IFRS 18. According to him, audit committees must also understand how changing regulatory expectations affect boards, companies and corporate accountability in Nigeria. Oputa said the 2026 summit, themed “Shaping High-Performing Audit Committees,” built on the success of its inaugural edition and provided a platform for audit committee members, board members, regulators, governance leaders and business executives to exchange perspectives on strengthening oversight and governance effectiveness. Nigeria’s economic outlook faces risks Meanwhile, Associate Partner, Strategy and Transactions, EY West Africa, Olayinka Oyetunji, said Nigeria’s economic growth outlook remained positive but faced significant downside risks from rising debt-servicing costs, insecurity and election-related uncertainty. She said approximately 43 per cent of government revenue was projected to go into debt servicing in 2026, limiting resources available for infrastructure and economic development. Oyetunji also noted that although Nigeria’s capital importation had increased, about 88 per cent represented foreign portfolio investment, underscoring the need to attract more sustainable foreign direct investment. She urged corporate boards to strengthen supply-chain resilience, diversify energy sources, prioritise investments and improve liquidity management. Oyetunji also drew attention to the Financial Reporting Council’s draft valuation regulation, expected to take effect on January 1, 2027, urging boards to ensure independent and credible asset valuations for financial reporting. items.title: Kidnapping: Afenifere seeks sophisticated weapons for Amotekun
items.description: …Demands drones, forest surveillance, grassroots intelligence, full LG autonomy By Adeola Badru The pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation, Afenifere, has called for a comprehensive overhaul of the South-West’s security architecture, urging governments to equip the Western Nigeria Security Network, codenamed Amotekun, with sophisticated weapons and modern surveillance technology to tackle kidnapping and other violent crimes. The organisation also called for the deployment of drones, improved forest surveillance, coordinated security operations and stronger grassroots intelligence gathering to curb the activities of kidnappers and armed gangs across the region. Afenifere warned that persistent attacks on highways, forests and rural communities exposed gaps in existing security arrangements, insisting that governments must move beyond security meetings and adopt more effective operational strategies. It further cautioned that poverty, educational deprivation and youth unemployment could sustain a recruitment pipeline for bandits and other criminal networks, urging authorities to combine security operations with sustained social and economic interventions. Afenifere’s National Publicity Secretary, Jare Ajayi, made the demands in a statement issued against the backdrop of recent abductions along the Ijebu-Ode–Ibadan highway and at the Forestry Research Institute of Nigeria, FRIN, Ibadan, on Wednesday. The latest incidents included the abduction of travellers heading to Ibadan from Ijebu-Ode, Ogun State, last Tuesday, with their abductors reportedly demanding a ransom of N25 million. One of the victims was identified as Mr Dapo, a recent National Youth Service Corps graduate who had just completed his national service in Edo State. The incident came weeks after prospective corps members travelling from Ibadan were abducted in Imo State on October 1, 2026. Similarly, the kidnapping of victims at FRIN, along the Ibadan–Ijebu-Ode highway, raised fresh concerns, as the location had reportedly witnessed a similar incident a few months earlier. Although the victims were eventually rescued or released, Afenifere said their freedom should not overshadow the recurring nature of the attacks and the threat they posed to residents, commuters and economic activities. Ajayi said, “We are deeply saddened that these disheartening incidents are occurring at all, as they remind us that much still needs to be done to secure the people and ensure their safety.” The organisation described the incidents as part of a disturbing pattern of violent crimes across the Yoruba-speaking states and adjoining areas. It cited the reported beheading of a farmer in Itesiwaju Local Government Area of Oyo State, the kidnapping of Prince Michael Folarin in Igbeti and the abduction of a 33-year-old poultry farmer, Mr Ooreoluwa Osonuga, in Ogun State. Afenifere also listed the abduction of Honourable Debo Farounbi in Ora, Osun State, alongside reported kidnapping incidents in parts of Kwara, Kogi and Niger states. According to the organisation, the geographical spread and recurring nature of the attacks made a coordinated regional security response imperative. It acknowledged security initiatives undertaken by South-West governments, including Operation Kosaye, launched by the Ogun and Lagos State governments, and tripartite security arrangements involving Lagos, Ogun and Oyo states. It also recalled a joint security meeting of governors held in Ibadan on November 25, 2025, noting that the engagements demonstrated recognition of the regional security challenge. However, Afenifere said the persistence of attacks despite the initiatives called for a fundamental reassessment of existing strategies. “While these efforts are acknowledged, the fact that insecurity, particularly kidnapping, persists on our land suggests that current measures are not enough. “There is a need for more focused, strategic, and better-coordinated actions from the authorities and security agencies in conjunction with local communities,” Ajayi stated. Education, poverty and insecurity Afenifere identified the growing number of out-of-school children and the vulnerability of disadvantaged youths as factors that could worsen the country’s security challenges. It cited concerns expressed by the Sultan of Sokoto, Alhaji Muhammad Sa’ad Abubakar III, over the high population of out-of-school children in Northern Nigeria and the implications for national security and development. The Sultan reportedly raised the concern at last Saturday’s Barewa Old Boys’ Association lecture in Gombe, entitled, “The Scourge of Out-of-School Children in Nigeria and the Implications for National Security and National Development”. Afenifere also recalled the Sultan’s December 9, 2024, remarks during the graduation ceremony of 1,897 Almajiri pupils and 1,087 out-of-school adolescent girls at the Sultan Maccido Institute of Quranic and General Studies in Sokoto. Represented by the Ciroma of Sokoto, Alhaji Aliyu Abubakar, the Sultan had warned that children neglected under the Almajiri system were vulnerable to exploitation and recruitment by criminal elements. He had also urged traditional rulers to take a firm position against street begging. Drawing parallels with the educational philosophy of the late Premier of the Western Region, Chief Obafemi Awolowo, Afenifere recalled his advocacy for mass education as an instrument of enlightenment and national development. The organisation said Awolowo had repeatedly warned during his political campaigns in 1959 and 1979 about the consequences of neglecting the education of young people. It quoted him as saying: “Northern youths may ask their leaders some questions when they see the rate of development that goes with education in many parts of Southern Nigeria.” Afenifere also recalled Awolowo’s position on intellectual development, particularly his assertion that “the power to think clearly, correctly, and scientifically is the greatest of all the powers that a man can possess.” Against this background, the organisation urged governments to increase investment in public education and establish effective welfare programmes to provide vulnerable children with access to schooling and social protection. It argued that poverty, lack of education and desperation could make disadvantaged young people susceptible to exploitation and recruitment by criminal organisations. Demands stronger security operations On the immediate security response, Afenifere urged South-West governments to provide Amotekun with modern, high-grade weapons capable of confronting heavily armed criminal gangs. It also proposed the integration of conventional security agencies and local security outfits into coordinated tactical squads to strengthen forest surveillance, patrol operations and responses to attacks in remote communities. The organisation called for the acquisition and deployment of drones, advanced communication gadgets and rapid-response equipment to monitor forests, border communities and other areas vulnerable to criminal infiltration. On local governance, it advocated full financial autonomy for local government councils, arguing that direct access to resources would enable grassroots administrations to support community policing and sustain regular security patrols in rural areas. Afenifere further recommended mechanised agricultural initiatives and vocational training programmes to provide sustainable livelihoods for young people and reduce their vulnerability to recruitment by criminal networks. It also called for strict enforcement of judicial penalties against kidnappers, bandits and perpetrators of violent crimes, maintaining that the justice system must serve as an effective deterrent. To strengthen intelligence gathering, the organisation proposed efficient grassroots reporting structures through which residents could promptly communicate suspicious activities to ward leaders, community heads and security agencies. It urged traditional rulers, including Obas and Baales, community leaders and security agencies to take proactive responsibility for local security by coordinating neighbourhood watch groups, monitoring new arrivals in rural settlements and maintaining functional early-warning mechanisms. Afenifere maintained that tackling the security crisis required a holistic approach combining effective policing, modern technology, community intelligence, judicial accountability and sustained investment in education and economic opportunities. items.title: Lattice Energy positions for growth in Ghana’s petroleum downstream industry
items.description: Ghanaian energy trading and supply company, Lattice Energy Ltd, says it is positioning itself to contribute to the growth of the country’s petroleum downstream industry through strategic petroleum sourcing, supply partnerships and commercial energy solutions. The company, a member of Abagona Legacy Holdings, says its expansion into the sector forms part of the Group’s broader ambition to build an integrated energy and logistics business with interests across the petroleum value chain. Lattice Energy’s entry into the market builds on the Group’s investments in logistics, petroleum marketing and engineering services, which began in 2017 with the establishment of Translogies, its haulage and logistics business. In 2019, the Group expanded into petroleum marketing through Sotei Energy Limited, an Oil Marketing Company (OMC) operating in Ghana. The addition of Lattice Energy is expected to strengthen coordination across petroleum sourcing, bulk supply, distribution and retail marketing, while creating opportunities for the Group to expand its footprint in the energy sector. Other businesses within the Group’s portfolio include Zupoil and Mataros Engineering, which reflect its interests in petroleum, logistics and engineering. In a statement, Lattice Energy said its business model focuses on sourcing petroleum products, developing strategic supplier relationships and providing supply solutions to commercial and industrial customers in Ghana and the wider West African market. It said the company intends to leverage strategic partnerships, operational coordination and its growing industry expertise to deliver dependable petroleum supply solutions while pursuing opportunities in regional energy trading. The company also expressed its ambition to build a commercially sustainable indigenous business capable of competing in an increasingly interconnected regional energy market. According to the statement, the Group intends to draw on its existing capabilities in logistics, petroleum marketing and engineering to improve operational efficiencies and explore new opportunities across the energy value chain. Abagona Legacy Holdings Chief Executive, David Azupio, leads the broader strategic direction of the Group’s growing business portfolio. Lattice Energy said it remains focused on strengthening petroleum supply networks, creating value for stakeholders and contributing to Ghana’s position in the West African energy market as it develops its operations and strategic partnerships. The company said it looks forward to engaging industry stakeholders, business partners and investors as it advances its growth plans.

items.title: TOR seeks private investors to shield refinery from political interference
items.description: The Tema Oil Refinery (TOR) is working to attract private-sector investors as part of efforts to strengthen its governance structure and protect the state-owned facility from political interference. Managing Director of TOR, Edmond Kombat , says opening up the refinery to private participation through a planned stock exchange listing will help secure its future and ensure continuity in its operations. Speaking on the second day of the Ghana Economic Forum organised by the Business & Financial Times (B&FT), he said the refinery is targeting a listing on the Ghana Stock Exchange in 2028. He explained that the involvement of private investors, including pension funds, could bring independent directors onto the board and strengthen corporate oversight. “If it is listed with some level of private participation, whether it’s private pension funds or any other, that brings independent directors on the board. It will be more secured and more sustainable,” he said. Mr Kombat believes the arrangement would make it more difficult for future political administrations to allow the refinery to collapse again. He also said the refinery’s workers and unions remain vigilant about its operations, adding that listing on the stock exchange is the best option for ensuring its long-term sustainability. “The best sustainability is to get it listed on the stock exchange,” he stressed.

items.title: From Idea to Printed Object: How AI Is Rewriting the 3D Modeling Workflow
items.description: A designer sketches a bracket on a napkin over lunch. By the time her coffee cools, she wants a printable version on her desk. Not long ago, that jump meant hours in CAD software or a hunt through forums for a model that almost fit. Today the path is shorter, and artificial intelligence is the reason. 3D printing has moved well beyond hobby circles. Small studios, product teams, educators, and indie game developers all use it for prototypes and finished parts. Yet one bottleneck has barely moved: getting a clean, printable model still takes skill and time. This article looks at how AI-driven modeling is closing that gap, what to look for in a platform, and how to build a workflow that holds up in real production. Why Modeling Is Still the Slowest Step in 3D Printing Printers have become faster, cheaper, and more reliable. Slicers have become friendlier. The model itself is often the weakest link, because building one from scratch demands training that many makers simply don’t have. Most people respond by borrowing. They browse libraries of free STL files , which works well when someone has already designed something close to what you need. The trouble starts when your project is specific: a custom enclosure, a unique figurine, or a part sized to an odd space. At that point you either learn modeling software or compromise on the design. Neither option scales when deadlines are tight. This gap between “I know what I want” and “I have a printable file” is where AI generation now earns its place. What AI 3D Model Generation Actually Does AI generators turn simple inputs into three-dimensional geometry. Instead of pushing vertices around, you describe the object or show the system a picture, and it builds a mesh for you. Meshy is one of the leading AI 3D model generators, and its approach shows how flexible the category has become. It offers two main modes. Text to 3D builds a model from a written description, while Image to 3D works from a reference photo or concept art. Image mode also accepts multiple images of the same object. Feeding it several angles gives the system more information about depth and form, which improves accuracy compared with a single view. For anyone recreating a real-world item, that difference matters. Built for the Browser, Open to Experimentation One of the biggest barriers in 3D work has always been setup. Heavy software, powerful hardware, and long installs discourage beginners and slow down busy professionals. Meshy runs entirely in the browser, so there is nothing to install. A free tier lets you test ideas before committing, which suits makers who want to see whether AI modeling fits their workflow. The platform also includes a free 3D Tool Kit with three utilities. The Converter changes file formats, the Online Viewer lets you inspect a model, and STL Repair fixes common mesh problems before printing. Export options cover STL, OBJ, GLB, and FBX, so the same asset can go to a printer, a game engine, or a design review without conversion headaches. From Prompt to Print: A Simple Five-Step Workflow A reliable process matters more than any single tool. Here is a practical sequence that works for most projects. Define the object. Write down size, purpose, and style before you generate anything. Specific prompts produce more usable results. Generate with text or images. Use text for original concepts and images when you are matching something that already exists. Inspect the result. Rotate the model in a viewer and look for thin walls, gaps, or floating parts. Repair and export. Run a repair pass, then export as STL for printing. Slice and test. Print a small draft first, adjust the prompt if needed, and then commit to the final run. Treat the first output as a draft. Iteration is cheap, so refining a prompt two or three times usually beats trying to perfect one attempt. Beyond Printing: Where Teams and Developers Benefit Printing is only one use for generated models. Game developers use AI to populate scenes with props and characters quickly. Meshy supports AI texturing and auto-rigging, so a static model can gain surface detail and a skeleton for animation without separate tools. Product designers use generated models as fast concept visuals before investing in engineering drawings. Educators use them to turn classroom ideas into objects students can hold. For technical teams, Meshy provides API access, which means generation can be built directly into an existing pipeline or app. A studio could, for example, let customers describe a custom item and receive a printable preview automatically. That kind of integration turns AI modeling from a standalone tool into part of a product. Frequently Asked Questions Do I need modeling experience to use AI 3D generation? No. Text and image inputs are designed for people without CAD training, though a basic understanding of printing constraints helps. Is a generated model ready to print immediately? Often it is close, but a quick inspection and repair pass is wise. Small mesh errors can cause failed prints. Can I use the same model for games and printing? Yes, provided the platform exports multiple formats. Choose STL for printers and GLB or FBX for game engines. Conclusion: A Faster, More Accessible Future for Making The pattern across all of this is clear. The hardest part of 3D printing has shifted from machines to models, and AI is the first technology to ease that pressure in a meaningful way. Text prompts, multi-image input, browser-based tools, and broad export support lower the cost of trying an idea. For makers and businesses, the long-term value goes beyond speed. When creating a model no longer demands years of training, more people can prototype, test, and refine their ideas. Teams spend less time wrestling with geometry and more time improving designs. As AI generation matures, expect tighter links between modeling, texturing, animation, and manufacturing. Platforms like Meshy point toward a future where describing an object is the first step of building it, and the gap between imagination and a physical result keeps shrinking. items.title: NIA to begin Ghana Card registration for children in Upper West, Savannah on November 12
items.description: The National Identification Authority (NIA), in collaboration with the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA), will begin the nationwide Ghana Card registration exercise for children aged six to 14 in the Upper West and Savannah Regions on Thursday, November 12. The exercise follows the successful completion of the registration in the Volta, Oti, Northern, Upper East and North-East Regions. In a statement issued on Wednesday, November 11, the NIA said registration teams would visit public and private schools to ensure extensive coverage, with the exercise taking place daily from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Children within the eligible age bracket who are not enrolled in school may register at designated centres or schools within their localities. Parents and guardians are required to present the child’s original birth certificate, valid Ghanaian passport or Certificate of Acquired Citizenship. Where these documents are unavailable, a parent, relative or legal guardian may complete an Oath of Identity form to facilitate registration. For children without known relatives, two Social Welfare Officers responsible for their welfare may vouch for them under oath. The NIA has also encouraged parents and guardians to provide the child’s National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) card or NHIS number, where available. It said anyone presenting a child for registration must be a Ghanaian aged at least 18, of sound mind and in possession of a valid Ghana Card. The Authority has urged parents, guardians, school authorities, traditional leaders and other community stakeholders in the two regions to support the exercise to ensure its success. It further cautioned that providing false information or facilitating the registration of a non-Ghanaian constitutes an offence punishable under the law. The NIA reaffirmed its commitment to providing a secure, inclusive and reliable national identification system for all Ghanaians.

Guinée : à Mali, 17 blessés, dont quatre militaires, après les manifestations d’élèves
items.description: Les manifestations d’élèves survenues le lundi 9 novembre 2026 à Mali, en Moyenne Guinée, ont fait 17 blessés, dont quatre militaires et deux femmes enceintes. Le maire de la commune urbaine dément par ailleurs toute fausse couche parmi les victimes. Joint au téléphone ce mercredi 11 novembre 2026, le maire de la commune urbaine de Mali, Mamadou Dian Dieng, est revenu sur les circonstances de ces incidents et le bilan sanitaire enregistré à l’hôpital préfectoral. « L’hôpital a reçu dix-sept (17) patients. Parmi eux, sept ont inhalé du gaz lacrymogène, tandis que dix autres ont été blessés par des jets de pierres. Parmi les victimes figurent également deux femmes enceintes, quatre militaires et deux commerçants », a précisé l’autorité communale. Le maire a également tenu à démentir une information faisant état d’une fausse couche qu’aurait subie l’une des femmes enceintes prises en charge à l’hôpital. « Nous démentissons cette information sur la base du rapport médical que nous avons reçu du directeur préfectoral de l’hôpital. C’est vrai que deux femmes enceintes ont été prises en charge parmi les victimes de ces douloureux événements, mais, jusqu’au moment où je vous parle, aussi bien les deux femmes que les enfants qu’elles portent se portent bien », a-t-il rassuré. Pour terminer, Mamadou Dian Dieng a invité les citoyens à privilégier les informations provenant des sources officielles et à éviter la propagation de fausses nouvelles autour de ces événements. Alpha Moussa Dieng, correspondant régional à Labé L’article Guinée : à Mali, 17 blessés, dont quatre militaires, après les manifestations d’élèves est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Centre for CSR West Africa urges greener festivals and concerts as festive season approaches
items.description: The Centre for CSR, West Africa, has urged event organisers in Ghana to adopt more environmentally responsible practices as the country approaches a season of festivals, concerts, corporate events and other celebrations. The Centre says the creative and events industry can help advance climate action by reducing waste, using resources more responsibly and rethinking how events are planned and produced. Delivering a goodwill message at the Climate x Culture Summit 2026 in Accra, Priscilla Adomaah Nsonwaah, representing the Centre, said the industry had an opportunity to demonstrate that memorable events could be organised without placing unnecessary pressure on the environment. “As we approach a season filled with festivals, concerts, corporate events and celebrations, we have an opportunity to ask ourselves: Can we create memorable experiences while also being kinder to our environment? I believe we can. And it starts with each of us,” she said on October 22. She stressed that climate action did not always require major interventions, noting that simple decisions such as reducing waste, using resources responsibly and rethinking event production could contribute to environmental sustainability. As one of the event sponsors, the Centre also expressed support for the proposed Accra Climate Culture Accord and the Sustainable Event Production Guide, describing them as initiatives that could help move climate conversations from awareness to practical action. According to Ms Nsonwaah, the initiatives could provide direction for more responsible event production across Ghana and Africa. She said organisations had responsibilities beyond their commercial activities, including obligations to the people, communities and environment within which they operate. Ms Nsonwaah further highlighted the role of culture and creativity in influencing public attitudes towards climate change, arguing that music, storytelling and creative campaigns could inspire behavioural change. She commended the organisers of the summit for bringing together stakeholders from the creative industry, media, business and climate advocacy to explore ways of integrating sustainability into cultural experiences. The Climate x Culture Summit 2026 was organised by CultureJoint in partnership with the Minister of State for Climate Change and Sustainability under the theme, “Designing Sustainable Creative Experiences for Africa.”

items.title: 2027: I’d have joined Rainbow Coalition if still in politics — Ladoja
items.description: By Adeola Badru The Olubadan of Ibadanland, Oba Rashidi Ladoja, has said he would have joined the Rainbow Coalition if he were still active in partisan politics, but noted that his position as a traditional ruler requires him to remain politically neutral. Ladoja said although he appreciated the political initiative behind the coalition, his traditional role demanded fairness, neutrality and equal treatment of all political tendencies, irrespective of party affiliations. The monarch spoke on Wednesday when he received a delegation of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) National Working Committee, led by the party’s National Secretary, Senator Samuel Anyanwu, at his palace in Ibadan. The delegation, which included members of the party’s national leadership and its governorship candidate in Oyo State, Hazeem Gbolarumi, paid homage to the monarch and formally presented the candidate to him ahead of the 2027 general elections. Speaking during the visit, Ladoja said his political disposition would have been different if he were still actively involved in partisan politics. “If I were still a politician, I would have joined the Rainbow Coalition. But now that I am a traditional ruler, my responsibility is different. “I have to accommodate everybody, irrespective of the political party they belong to. I cannot take sides with any political party or candidate. My duty is to receive everybody, advise them and admonish them where necessary,” the monarch said. He stressed that traditional rulers had important roles to play in sustaining democratic stability, particularly during electioneering periods, adding that their influence should be deployed towards promoting peaceful political engagement rather than deepening divisions. The Olubadan also said Nigeria needed a trusted leader capable of commanding public confidence, inspiring national unity and providing purposeful leadership amid the country’s numerous challenges. According to him, the country requires leadership anchored on credibility, integrity and the ability to earn the trust of the people. He urged politicians to place national interest above personal ambitions and partisan considerations, stressing that the political process should be guided by responsibility and genuine commitment to national development. Ladoja also appealed to political stakeholders to conduct themselves in ways that would preserve the peace and stability of the country as preparations for the 2027 general elections gather momentum. Earlier, Anyanwu said the PDP delegation’s visit was part of efforts to sustain the party’s relationship with traditional institutions and seek the monarch’s royal blessings and counsel ahead of the next general elections. He reaffirmed the group’s recognition of the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, as the national leader of the PDP, insisting that its political direction remained firmly anchored on the Rainbow Coalition. Anyanwu said the coalition was established to promote political cooperation and build a broader platform for addressing the country’s political and developmental challenges. He declared that the PDP leadership aligned with the initiative would sustain its commitment to the coalition and work with like-minded political forces ahead of the 2027 elections. “We remain committed to the Rainbow Coalition formed by the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike. “We recognise him as the national leader of our party, and we are committed to the political direction he has provided,” Anyanwu said. The PDP national secretary also reaffirmed the group’s support for President Bola Tinubu’s second-term ambition, describing it as part of its political commitment ahead of the 2027 presidential election. He said the party’s engagements with political stakeholders and traditional rulers were aimed at strengthening understanding, consolidating alliances and securing wider acceptance for its political direction. Anyanwu added that the PDP would continue to engage relevant stakeholders across the country to strengthen its political structures and advance its interests ahead of the forthcoming elections. The visit also provided an opportunity for the delegation to formally introduce Gbolarumi, the party’s governorship candidate in Oyo State, to the Olubadan. The delegation sought the monarch’s royal blessings, goodwill and fatherly guidance, expressing confidence in the party’s political aspirations in the state.
