items.title: PM Shehbaz highlights Pakistan's solar 'revolution by ordinary citizens' at COP31
items.description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday highlighted Pakistan’s solar power boom at the COP31 in Turkiye, where world leaders gathered to discuss joint solutions to combat climate change. This year’s summit focuses on transitioning toward a low-carbon future. Delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya as global greenhouse gas emissions show little sign of falling and wars, inflation and other crises compete for political attention. Addressing a high-level dialogue on clean energy transition, titled ‘ 35 by 35: Powering the Future ’, PM Shehbaz said : “In my country, an extraordinary transition has already taken place. “In just two years, Pakistan has added nearly 22 gigawatts of rooftop solar capacity — a quiet revolution by ordinary citizens seeking affordable power and a cleaner, more predictable future.” He affirmed that Pakistan fully supports the ‘ 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge ’, wherein countries agree to aim to increase electricity’s share of total final energy consumption to around 35 per cent by 2035 in line with global climate objectives. The premier recalled the recent inauguration of a “key section” of Pakistan’s seventh nuclear power plant, Chashma-5, referring to its dome placement. He explained that the project will add 1,200 megawatts of clean energy to Pakistan’s energy mix. “A second transformation is now underway on our roads and highways. Clean sources now provide nearly 55pc of our energy mix,” PM Shehbaz declared. The prime minister then highlighted that Pakistan’s newly drafted auto policy builds on the country’s aim to have 30pc of its new vehicles be electric by 2030 by offering “incentives for them through lower tariffs”. “All future government buses and motorcycles will be electric. This year, for the first time, more than one in every 10 motorcycles sold in Pakistan was electric,” he stated. “The momentum is real and it is accelerating,” PM Shehbaz remarked, while cautioning that “momentum without finance cannot be sustained”. “Our grids must expand quickly and reliably. Storage must keep supply steady. New technologies must be affordable for all. Yet, this burden falls on countries already under heavy debt,” he emphasised. The prime minister noted that Pakistan alone needs around $138 billion by 2035 for low-carbon power and $50 billion more to replace coal with solar. He stated that the ‘35 by 35’ clean energy goal could only be achieved “if finance flows at the speed of ambition through concessional capital and the transfer of affordable technology”. “Let us resolve to power our economies without impoverishing our people and light up our homes without darkening our planet. That is the promise of 35 by 35, and it is a promise we must deliver together and under all circumstances,” the premier remarked. He thanked Turkiye President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, whose country has the COP31 presidency, for convening the “important dialogue”. Earlier in the day, PM Shehbaz was received by Erdogan and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres upon his arrival at the venue, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said. The premier and other world leaders then gathered for a group photograph at the summit. In his speech at the Antalya Leaders’ Summit, PM Shehbaz will highlight Pakistan’s climate priorities and emphasise the urgent need for enhanced global climate action and strengthened international cooperation to mitigate the adverse impacts of climate change, according to PMO. The Foreign Office (FO) said the prime minister will also highlight “Pakistan’s steps towards rapid solarisation and expansion of its renewable energy capacity, as part of its transition towards a cleaner and more resilient economy, along with its efforts to strengthen disaster preparedness and early-warning systems”. He will call for predictable, adequate and accessible climate finance for developing countries to strengthen their resilience and pursue sustainable development, it added. According to the PMO, a “Pakistan Pavilion” has been established at the COP31 venue where 54 events will be hosted on various themes. Turkiye’s Erdogan highlights Gaza ‘ecocide’ Dozens of leaders were to speak during the “ high-level segment ” taking place on Wednesday and Thursday, including Erdogan, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, whose country hosted last year’s climate talks. “Nature — no less than people — is also paying a heavy price for armed conflicts. The starkest example of this is Gaza… what has taken place in Gaza is not only a genocide, but it is also an ecocide,” Erdogan said to applause. Turkiye did not invite Israel to COP31, The Jerusalem Post reported . “As the host country for the leaders’ summit, we did not send an invitation to Israel,” it quoted Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum as saying. “Of course, we will discuss the climate and climate justice here. We say that there can be no climate justice where peace does not prevail.” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, and the United Kingdom’s PM Andy Burnham were also scheduled to speak on Wednesday. The United States, the world’s largest historical emitter, has skipped the talks for the second year in a ‌row after ⁠President Donald Trump — who has called global warming a hoax — withdrew the US from climate cooperation following his return to office in 2025. Negotiators from nearly 200 countries are seeking agreement on a plan to increase the share of electricity in global energy use and revive stalled efforts to move away from fossil fuels. As the third day began, the UN chief told world leaders at the summit that the slow international response to climate change so far had placed the world on a path to destruction. Governments must fight harder to preserve the planet for future generations, he said, in comments that set the tone for two days of rapid-fire speeches by world leaders. “The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us. This is the path to mutually assured destruction,” Guterres said, pointing to rising emissions, global temperatures and worsening climate-driven disasters. “But science is not telling us to surrender. It is telling us to fight harder.” PM meets world leaders On the sidelines of the summit, the prime minister held conversations with leaders of various countries and international bodies. The premier and his delegation also had a separate meeting with Iran’s Pezeshkian and his team. The meeting was to “discuss bilateral relations and the promotion of mutual cooperation between Pakistan and Iran”, as well as the regional situation and matters related to regional peace, PMO stated. PM Shehbaz, in a post on X, said he was “delighted to meet my brother”. While reaffirming the “deep and enduring bonds” between the two neighbours, the prime minister said he “conveyed Pakistan’s deep concern over the prolonged conflict in our region”. “Dialogue, restraint, de-escalation and sustained diplomacy are the only path to lasting peace,” he stressed. “Building on the understandings reached under the Islamabad MoU, Pakistan continues to play a sincere and constructive role for peace and stability in the region and beyond.” PM Shehbaz also met with Kuwait’s PM Ahmad Al-Abdullah Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah, with both leaders discussing the longstanding fraternal relations between their countries. They “reaffirmed their resolve to further strengthen cooperation in a range of areas of mutual interest, including trade, investment, energy, development cooperation and people-to-people exchanges”, PMO said. The two premiers expressed the hope that the recent ratification of the Pak-Kuwait defence agreement would “further promote bilateral cooperation”. They also exchanged views on international developments and challenges to regional peace. PM Shehbaz’s informal meetings included those with Bangladesh’s PM Tarique Rehman, Palestinian PM Mohammad Mustafa, Saudi Energy Minister Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, Saudi State Minister for Foreign Affairs Adel bin Ahmed al-Jubeir and Syria’s President Ahmed al-Sharaa, according to PMO. He also met Organisation of Islamic Cooperation chief Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed, World Bank President Ajay Banga and Türkiye’s First Lady Emine Erdoğan. In his conversation with his Palestinian counterpart, PM Shehbaz expressed Pakistan’s full solidarity with Palestinians. According to PMO, Mustafa thanked the government and people of Pakistan for “effectively raising their voices on the global level against the injustices inflicted on the Palestinian people and for supporting the Palestinian stance”. “During these cordial meetings, the prime minister and the world leaders discussed strengthening bilateral relations and the situation in the region,” PMO said. It added that the meetings also stressed the importance of highlighting the challenges faced by countries most affected by climate change at the international level. Year of extreme weather A UN report last month found the world on course to break through the 1.5 degrees Celsius warming limit that countries had agreed to pursue under the Paris Agreement to prevent the worst effects of climate change. Meanwhile, 2026 has also stood out with a series of extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a catastrophic flood killing more than 1,450 people, with thousands still missing. Former French prime minister Laurent Fabius, who presided over the 2015 Paris climate conference and leads an advisory council of former COP presidents, said on Tuesday the leaders’ speeches should give political impetus to the negotiations. “It is an opportunity for leaders to make some announcements, and more this time, to explain how they will implement, because the key word in Antalya is implementation,” he told Reuters. Several other nations, including France, Germany, Japan, Italy and Canada, did not send their top leaders to the talks this year and won’t be represented in the speeches. “The world’s biggest economies should be leading the response to the climate crisis, not leaving it to others,” said Mohamed Adow, director of climate and energy think tank Power Shift Africa. Age of electricity? COP31 host Turkiye has been pushing for countries to put a goal on electrification at the centre of a final deal, though critics say it may do little to curb warming. The proposal targets a rise in electricity’s share of total global energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035, up from a little over a fifth now, theoretically reducing greenhouse gas emissions from cars, factories and buildings. But the proposal does not include language requiring new power to be generated by clean energy sources, and governments have yet to clarify a broader plan to transition away from fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas. Guterres urged countries to speed their transition to clean energy sources. He said the world’s dependence on fossil fuels was also damaging economies, not just the climate, an apparent nod to surging petroleum prices since the start of the US and Israeli war against Iran that has disrupted Middle East oil exports. “Three-quarters of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did not create and cannot control,” he said. “Recent conflicts make clear that this is a recipe for chronic insecurity and a cost-of-living meltdown.” ‘Difficult start’ Ahead of the conference, negotiators had been locked in discussions late on Sunday over demands by developing nations to include items on climate finance in the official agenda. “This has already been a difficult start for COP31,” said Jasper Inventor, head of Greenpeace’s COP31 delegation. Under UN climate agreements, developed countries, which are historically responsible for most greenhouse gas emissions, have provided financial support to help developing nations adapt to climate impacts and transition to cleaner energy. But poorer countries say the sums remain insufficient. Inventor said developed countries were “taking a hard line” over whether to include a platform, agreed at COP30 in Brazil last year , aimed at discussing how wealthy nations should provide funds to developing nations. African countries are also pushing for the agenda to include discussions on the tripling of adaptation finance, which aims to help poorer nations pay for measures such as building sea walls or planting drought-resistant crops. Observers say few major breakthroughs are expected at COP31 as countries grapple with an oil price shock and geopolitical tensions fuelled by the US war on Iran and Russia’s conflict in Ukraine.

items.title: Régularisation fiscale à 8 % : une autre catégorie d’entreprises concernée
items.description: Une autre catégorie d'entreprises s'ajoute à la liste de celles concernées par le dispositif de régularisation fiscale volontaire à 8 % . Le dispositif est, pour rappel, institué par la loi de finances pour 2026. Il prévoit la régularisation des fonds non déclarés au fisc moyennant une imposition unique de 8 %. La possibilité de régularisation est ouverte aux personnes physiques ou morales non enregistrées auprès des autorités fiscales, à celles identifiées auprès de l'administration fiscale mais qui n'ont pas rempli leurs obligations de déclaration et de paiement, ainsi qu'à celles qui déposent régulièrement leurs déclarations fiscales, mais dont les bases fiscales déclarées comportent des insuffisances. Voici les contribuables exclus de la régularisation volontaire Outre les personnes physiques ou morales détenant des fonds provenant d’activités constituant des infractions pénales, en particulier celles liées au blanchiment d’argent en lien avec le financement du terrorisme, la corruption ou les activités interdites, le dispositif exclut aussi plusieurs catégories de sociétés. Il s’agit de celles relevant de la Direction des Grandes Entreprises (DGE), de celles ayant réalisé un chiffre d'affaires de plus de 2 milliards de dinars au 31 décembre 2025, des entreprises du secteur pétrolier, des sociétés à capitaux étrangers , les entreprises étrangères qui ne disposent pas d'une résidence permanente en Algérie, des sociétés de tabacs, de pierres précieuses ou de métaux précieux ainsi que de celles ayant passé des contrats avec les opérateurs de téléphonie mobile, comme indiqué dans une circulaire de la Direction Générale des Impôts (DGI) émise le 5 avril dernier. Les entreprises ayant réalisé plus de 2 milliards de DA avant 2025 concernées Devant les questions soulevées par les directions de wilayas, la DGI vient d’émettre une nouvelle circulaire précisant que les entreprises exclues sont celles ayant réalisé un chiffre d'affaires annuel déclaré au 31 décembre 2025, égal ou supérieur à 2 milliards de dinars. Dans ses explications, la DGI a indiqué que les entreprises ayant enregistré des chiffres d'affaires annuels égaux ou supérieurs au seuil en question, au titre des exercices antérieurs à l'année 2025, peuvent bénéficier, sur leur demande, de la régularisation volontaire. Autre précision importante de la Direction des Impôts : les autres catégories d'entreprises exclues du dispositif ne peuvent aucunement y souscrire, même si leurs chiffres d'affaires de l'année 2025 sont inférieurs au seuil de 2 milliards de dinars. L’article Régularisation fiscale à 8 % : une autre catégorie d’entreprises concernée est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
items.description: Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day. Although the American side said they saw “some openings”, there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia’s invasion. Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine’s negotiating team said that this round of talks – the first since February – “was one of the hardest.” “I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion,” he said. But he added that he felt “good momentum” and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible. Both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon. After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner – President Donald Trump’s son-in-law – would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky. This latest round of talks had been framed as centred around the “security architecture” of Europe. For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member. For Moscow, it is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe – a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance’s eastward expansion. Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to “create a new framework” of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could “secure lasting peace”, while Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said the world needed a “new” and “fair” security system. Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration’s commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin. Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin – with whom the EU does not officially communicate – said its delegation had not had any contact with them. Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent. Many – particularly in eastern Europe – feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented “if no consensus can be reached among Nato members,” a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday. Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them “added to the format” would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin. There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted. Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur “until there’s an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues,” he added. Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine’s eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas. This matter was the “hardest”, Kushner acknowledged, while Zelensky’s chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region. “These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex,” Kushner said. “The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this.”

items.title: Simandou : le président Doumbouya invite les investisseurs et durcit le ton sur le respect des règles
items.description: Lors d’un panel organisé après son discours d’ouverture du Simandou Mining Summit, mercredi 11 novembre sur l’île de Kassa, le président Mamadi Doumbouya a appelé les investisseurs à s’engager dans le programme Simandou 2040. Il a aussi reconnu que la Guinée avait fait preuve d’indulgence et affirmé qu’elle veillerait désormais au respect de ses règles. « On a été un peu indulgent », a déclaré Mamadi Doumbouya au terme de son intervention, en évoquant le panafricanisme. « À partir de maintenant, on veille au respect des règles et au respect de notre pays. Et ça, nous n’avons ni amis ni parents », a-t-il ajouté, sans nommer de pays ni d’entreprise. Quelques instants plus tôt, le chef de l’État avait invité les investisseurs institutionnels présents dans la salle à se sentir chez eux en Guinée. « Le programme Simandou 2040 vous offre des projets stratégiques bancables », leur a-t-il dit, en promettant « un cadre d’investissement attractif, des règles stables et la sécurité de vos investissements ». « Venez bâtir avec nous un partenariat gagnant-gagnant », a-t-il poursuivi. Le président est également revenu sur la création de la Compagnie du TransGuinéen, qui réunit l’État et ses partenaires miniers autour du chemin de fer et du port de Simandou. Évoquant les rapports entre les partenaires, dont Rio Tinto et Winning Consortium, il a affirmé que « les ennemis d’hier sont aujourd’hui devenus les meilleurs amis ». Interrogé sur les raisons pour lesquelles la Guinée détient 15 % de la société, Mamadi Doumbouya a défendu cette participation en faisant valoir l’absence d’apport financier de l’État. « La Guinée n’a pas mis un franc dedans », a-t-il déclaré. Il a présenté la société commune comme un moyen de partager les coûts et les risques tout en donnant à la Guinée une place d’actionnaire. Pour illustrer l’avancement du projet, le président a cité les expéditions de minerai et la formation des conducteurs de train. « Simandou n’est plus dans les tiroirs, Simandou est dans les bateaux », a-t-il lancé. Au-delà des expéditions, Mamadi Doumbouya a insisté sur la place que les Guinéens doivent prendre dans la conduite du projet. « La finalité, c’est quoi ? C’est le transfert d’expériences », a-t-il dit, en évoquant le chemin de fer, le port et, à terme, la transformation du minerai en Guinée, notamment à travers une aciérie. Il a dit vouloir que les Guinéens deviennent « surtout les décideurs ». Rappelant que les ressources minières finiront par s’épuiser, il a présenté Simandou comme un projet destiné aux générations futures. Il a également dit avoir consacré son mandat à la formation et à l’autonomie des femmes et des jeunes. « Je vous donne rendez-vous dans quinze ans. Vous allez trouver d’autres présidents », a-t-il lancé.

items.title: JOJ Dakar 2026 : deux médailles de bronze pour le Niger en taekwondo
items.description: Les jeunes taekwondoïstes nigeriens, Housseina Zada Mamoudou, dans la categorie des moins de 49 kg chez les dames, et Abdoul Aziz Issifi Mamoudou, chez les hommes de moins de 55 kg, ont chacun decroche une medaille de bronze lundi aux Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse de Dakar 2026. Les deux representants nigeriens ont realise un beau parcours dans leurs categories respectives avant de s'incliner en demi-finale face a leurs adversaires de la Republique de Coree et de l'Ouzbekistan. Housseina Zada Mamoudou revient sur son combat en demie finale face a la coreenne Lee Siwo : « c'est une medaille que je dedie avant tout a toute la population nigerienne et j'en suis fiere. C'est n'etait pas facile mais je suis arrive jusqu'au bout et j'ai beaucoup appris aussi, certaines techniques et des penalites que je ne connaissais pas avant. » Malgre ces defaites aux portes de la finale, Housseina Zada Mamoudou, et Abdoul Aziz Issifi Mamoudou permettent au Niger de monter a deux reprises sur le podium dans cette discipline. Une victoire qu'Issifi Mamoudou Abdoul Aziz dit y avoir longtemps prepare : « j'ai travaille depuis 2022 pour cette medaille donc c'est exceptionnel et un merite meme si j'ai souhaite la medaille en or. Je me suis certes incline en demie finale mais mon adversaire de l'Ouzbekistan est aussi de taille et a plus de chance que moi. Ce sont les regles des jeux on gagne comme on perd. C'est une grande experience pour moi et j'apprendrai de mes erreurs pour m'ameliorer et avancer. » Une performance encourageante pour le taekwondo nigerien, qui confirme ainsi le potentiel de sa jeune generation sur la scene sportive internationale, apres la medaille d'argent historique d'Abdoulrazak Issoufou Alfaga aux Jeux olympiques de Rio en 2016. Photo : OIS/Nic Bothma

items.title: 71% want jobs and youth employment prioritised in 2027 Budget – KPMG/UNDP survey
items.description: More than seven in 10 respondents want job creation and youth employment prioritised in Ghana’s 2027 Budget, according to a survey conducted by KPMG and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). The findings show that 71 per cent of respondents consider jobs and youth unemployment a top national priority for the government, while 54 per cent identify the cost of living as another major concern. The survey, which draws on responses from citizens and businesses as well as focus group discussions, highlights expectations for the 2027 Budget and the economic challenges facing households and enterprises. On taxation, 90 per cent of respondents want government to communicate changes at least four months before implementation to give businesses sufficient time to plan. The report says tax concerns extend beyond statutory rates to include complex filing processes, payments to multiple authorities and changes announced at short notice. “Tax-related concerns extend beyond statutory rates. Respondents identified complex filing, payments to multiple authorities and short-notice changes as significant impediments,” the report stated. It added that the leading preference for encouraging informal businesses to join the formal economy was increased education and awareness, followed by incentives for formalisation and aligning licensing processes with tax registration. The survey findings point to optimism among businesses, but also identify continuing constraints involving access to suitable financing, reliable utilities and market demand. Respondents expressed conditional interest in the government’s 24-Hour Economy programme, while highlighting job creation, youth employment and cash-flow challenges as important concerns. The report argues that policy measures should address the practical conditions businesses need to expand, invest and create employment. Drawing on the survey and focus group findings, KPMG and UNDP identify four priority areas for consideration in the 2027 Budget. These include enabling enterprise growth through affordable financing and predictable taxation, and translating the 24-Hour Economy programme and New Economy agenda into productive investment. The report also recommends improving the value of public investment and strengthening financial discipline, with effective coordination through the Value for Money Office. A fourth priority is safeguarding natural resources and accelerating green investment. The recommendations are intended to inform discussions on the 2027 Budget, with emphasis on feasible investment, effective implementation and measurable outcomes for businesses and communities.

items.title: Orpaillage clandestin à Siguiri – « Je ne sais rien de cette affaire », déclare l’ex-gouverneur Fadjimba Mara, qui plaide non coupable
items.description: L’ancien gouverneur de la région administrative de Siguiri, Fadjimba Mara, a rejeté les accusations portées contre lui dans l’affaire de l’orpaillage clandestin à Siguiri. À la barre de la Cour de répression des infractions économiques et financières (CRIEF), ce mercredi 11 novembre 2026, l’ancien officier a affirmé n’avoir jamais été informé de la présence d’orpailleurs étrangers sur les sites concernés. Les débats dans l’affaire opposant le parquet spécial aux 224 personnes interpellées pour leur implication présumée dans l’exploitation illégale de l’or à Siguiri se sont ouverts ce mercredi devant la chambre de jugement de la CRIEF. Les prévenus, tous placés sous mandat de dépôt, sont répartis en deux catégories : 22 administrateurs territoriaux et 202 personnes poursuivies pour orpaillage clandestin. Ces dernières sont de nationalités guinéenne, malienne, burkinabè, togolaise et béninoise. C’est l’ancien gouverneur de la région, Fadjimba Mara, colonel radié des effectifs de l’armée guinéenne, qui a ouvert le bal des auditions. Interrogé sur les faits qui lui sont reprochés, il a plaidé non coupable. « Je ne sais rien de cette affaire. Quand j’ai été informé de l’interdiction de l’exploitation illégale des mines, j’ai convoqué plusieurs réunions au cours desquelles nous avons pris des dispositions. Ces mesures avaient abouti à la fermeture de deux sites. Je n’étais même pas informé qu’il y avait des étrangers sur les sites. Nous, nous avons trouvé que les poclains avaient déjà détruit Siguiri et, actuellement, aucun de ces engins ne travaille là-bas », a-t-il déclaré. L’ancien gouverneur est poursuivi pour des faits présumés de complicité de dégradation de l’environnement, de destructions diverses et de pollution des eaux. Invité à s’expliquer sur son traitement salarial et son patrimoine, Fadjimba Mara a indiqué qu’il percevait un salaire mensuel de 7 millions de francs guinéens. Il a également déclaré posséder un bâtiment à Kissidougou, acquis en 2008, ainsi que deux terrains dans la même localité depuis 2010. « Je n’ai aucun véhicule personnel », a-t-il précisé. Elisa Camara L’article Orpaillage clandestin à Siguiri – « Je ne sais rien de cette affaire », déclare l’ex-gouverneur Fadjimba Mara, qui plaide non coupable est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: TOR targets listing on Ghana Stock Exchange by 2028 to ensure long-term sustainability
items.description: The Tema Oil Refinery (TOR) is targeting a listing on the Ghana Stock Exchange by 2028 as part of efforts to secure its long-term sustainability and prevent a recurrence of its operational challenges. Managing Director of TOR, Edmond Kombat says management is working to clean the refinery’s balance sheet, restructure its debt and achieve sustained profitability ahead of the planned listing. “We want to clean it and move to a positive equity and restructure the debt and we are targeting 2028 to list it,” he said. Speaking on the second day of the Ghana Economic Forum organised by the Business & Financial Times (B&FT), Mr Kombat said the refinery is targeting at least three consecutive years of sustained profitability before the listing. “We want to make sure at least we have three years sustained profitability,” he stated. He disclosed that TOR inherited negative equity of GH¢7.5 billion, which had reduced to GH¢5 billion by the end of 2025. “We cleaned the balance sheet because we had inherited a negative equity of 7.5 billion. At end of 2025, it came down to 5 billion,” he said. Mr Kombat believes bringing private investors, including pension funds, on board will strengthen the refinery’s corporate governance and protect it against political interference. “If it is listed with some level of private participation, whether it’s private pension funds or any other, that brings independent directors on the board. It will be more secured and more sustainable,” he explained. He described the proposed listing as the strongest guarantee of the refinery’s long-term survival. “The best sustainability is to get it listed on the stock exchange,” he stressed. On competition in the downstream petroleum market, Mr Kombat said TOR must focus on efficiency, product quality and competitive pricing to remain relevant. “What will save you in an open market is your quality and then your price. So we have to run the organisation professionally and make sure that we take our customers seriously,” he said. He also rejected suggestions that Bulk Distribution Companies (BDCs) pose a threat to the refinery, describing them instead as partners in its operations. “I don’t see the BDCs as an attainment to TOR. I see them as extensions of TOR because they distribute, they buy and distribute. They are not refining,” he added.

items.title: Un financement français : 41 millions d’euros pour améliorer et développer les services d’eau à Nouakchott et Nouadhibou
items.description: La Mauritanie et la France ont signé ce mercredi un accord de financement d'un montant de 41 millions d'euros (environ 1,854 milliard MRU), destiné à l'amélioration et au développement des services d'eau potable et au renforcement de l'efficacité des réseaux de distribution à Nouakchott et Nouadhibou. L'accord a été signé, du côté mauritanien, par le ministre des Affaires économiques et du Développement, Mouhamedou Ahmedou Mhaimid, et, du côté français, par l'ambassadeur Emmanuel Besnier et le directeur du bureau de l'Agence française de développement à Nouakchott, Inias Monkam Dafera. Cet accord vise à réduire les pertes techniques et commerciales dans les réseaux d’eau, à réhabiliter et installer 150 000 raccordements domestiques, ce qui permettra d’améliorer l’approvisionnement en eau pour environ 1,6 million d’habitants, en particulier dans les quartiers précaires et les périphéries urbaines, selon les informations fournies par le ministère des Affaires économiques et du Développement. Le ministère a ajouté que le projet vise également à renforcer la résilience des infrastructures hydrauliques face au changement climatique et à améliorer les performances techniques et institutionnelles de la Société nationale de l’eau. Le ministre des Affaires économiques et du Développement a déclaré que ce projet s’inscrit dans le cadre des efforts visant à améliorer l’accès des populations urbaines et rurales aux services essentiels et à renforcer les institutions publiques stratégiques, soulignant que le taux d’accès aux services d’eau en Mauritanie a dépassé 77 %. De son côté, l’ambassadeur de France a déclaré que ce financement reflétait l’engagement de son pays à accompagner les priorités de développement de la Mauritanie, soulignant que le montant total de l’aide financière française au pays, à travers l’Agence française de développement, s’élevait à environ 500 millions d’euros, l’accent étant mis sur les secteurs de l’eau et de l’assainissement.

items.title: Nadra launches chatbot that tells families exact papers needed for succession certificates
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Families dealing with inheritance can now get the exact process and list of documents for their case from an automated chatbot, introduced on the revamped succession website of the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra). The chatbot, called “ID”, works in Urdu and English on any phone or computer. It asks the user a few simple questions about the deceased, the legal heirs and the assets, and then generates on its own the steps to follow and a checklist of only those documents that the particular case needs. No Nadra official is involved in the exchange. Nadra spokesman Syed Shabahat Ali said the chatbot runs entirely online through a series of questions and answers, without asking for CNIC numbers or other personal details. Heirs living abroad are guided to complete their biometric verification online through the Pak ID facility. The chatbot also tells users which office can take up their case. It warns them early if the matter will have to go to court, such as when an heir is a minor or the heirs are in dispute. The chatbot interface advises the public to use it as a reference tool only, and to “always confirm final requirements” with the nearest Nadra registration centre. The authority has been issuing succession certificates and letters of administration in uncontested cases since 2021. The chatbot offers guidance before the applicant reaches a Nadra office with a formal application. Almost every family in Pakistan has to go through succession at some point, yet the requirements differ from case to case. The law varies with the faith and sect of the deceased, and the procedure changes from province to province. Sindh, for instance, requires three newspaper advertisements, while other jurisdictions require two. Many applicants usually learn such details only at a Nadra counter, often after travelling from another city. A screengrab from Nadra’s succession website. — succession.nadra.gov.pk The website makes it clear that Nadra can issue a succession certificate or letter of administration only in uncontested cases, where all legal heirs agree and have no dispute among them, no heir is a minor or mentally disabled, and the matter is neither pending before a court nor already decided by one. The deceased must be in Nadra’s records and the heirs must be registered in the Family Registration Certificate (FRC), while the applicant must hold a valid CNIC, Nadra card or Pakistan Origin Card (POC), as the old manual NIC is no longer accepted. A legal heir has to visit a Nadra centre in person, except in Sindh and Balochistan, where a lawyer can appear on his behalf. If any condition is not fulfilled, Nadra does not issue the certificate and the family has to approach the court. For an application to be accepted, the family has to produce the death certificate of the deceased issued by the relevant union council, municipal authority or cantonment board, along with the receipt of cancellation of the deceased’s CNIC, FRC, and copies of the CNICs of all legal heirs. They also need a Schedule-I letter of authorisation attested by an oath commissioner, and the original property documents, as photocopies are not accepted. In some cases, additional documents are required. For immovable property in Sindh, a search certificate has to be obtained, while in Sindh and Balochistan, a wakalatnama (power of attorney) is also required if the application is filed through a lawyer. If the deceased was a government or private employee, a letter from the concerned department about pension or service dues is also needed. The fee for a succession certificate or letter of administration is Rs10,000 where total assets are less than Rs100,000, and Rs20,000 where assets are Rs100,000 or more, except in Sindh where it is Rs22,000. A duplicate certificate costs Rs5,000.

items.title: Mondial U17 : Souleymane Commissaire Faye, le grand absent de la liste des Lionceaux
items.description: Le sélectionneur national des moins de 17 ans, Lamine Sané, a dévoilé les 21 joueurs retenus pour représenter le Sénégal à la Coupe du monde U17, prévue au Qatar du 19 novembre au 13 décembre 2026. Parmi les absences les plus remarquées figure celle de Souleymane « Commissaire » Faye, pourtant considéré comme l'un des jeunes talents de cette génération. La confirmation des effectifs par la FIFA met fin aux interrogations sur la présence du milieu offensif dans le groupe sénégalais. Son nom ne figure pas sur la liste définitive communiquée par l'instance mondiale. Cette décision surprend au regard du parcours du jeune joueur. Lors du tournoi UFOA-A U17 disputé en septembre dernier, il avait inscrit trois buts et participé au parcours des Lionceaux, qui avaient terminé à la deuxième place après leur défaite en finale contre la Gambie aux tirs au but. Lire aussi : Coupe du monde U17: La FIFA officialise la liste de l’équipe du Sénégal Depuis cette compétition, Souleymane Commissaire Faye n'avait plus retrouvé la sélection et n'avait pas pris part aux derniers regroupements préparatoires au Mondial. Les raisons précises de son absence de la liste définitive n'ont toutefois pas été officiellement communiquées. Au Qatar, les Lionceaux évolueront dans le groupe F avec la Croatie, Cuba et le Tadjikistan. Ils tenteront de défendre les couleurs sénégalaises dans cette compétition mondiale sans l'un des joueurs qui avaient marqué les esprits lors des précédentes échéances. C.T.N

items.title: Modi Is Losing His Grip on Dissent
items.description: F or more than a decade, Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government has relied on fear to throttle dissent in India. It has jailed protesters, deployed a pliant media to vilify critics, and fanned the flames of communal violence . This year, that playbook appears to have lost its efficacy. Discontent has grown, and Modi’s power no longer seems unassailable. The first signs of this change emerged over the summer. Tens of thousands of young people thronged Delhi to demand that India’s education minister resign. They had come of age in a country where public education was crumbling, economic growth favored the rich, and jobs were scarce . They had little patience for news channels perceived to be government mouthpieces—they even heckled several reporters out of their demonstrations. The summer’s young demonstrators mounted posters and circulated cheeky memes and slogans that took direct aim at the prime minister. When police attacked one of their marches with pellet guns, tear gas, and shock batons , the violence stoked public indignation that swelled the movement’s ranks. Modi then tried to endear himself with the digital-age protesters: He implored them to stand down in an Instagram selfie video, and his colleagues from the Hindu-nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party delivered speeches peppered with youthful slang, such as delulu and clock it . These efforts just earned the BJP more mockery . The police have used force against protesters before, but the effects were very different. In 2019, the BJP championed a discriminatory citizenship law; demonstrations erupted, and the police used brutal means to crush them, including abetting and even participating in communal violence . The following year, the government announced sweeping agricultural reforms. Farmers who protested that these favored giant corporations faced a violent crackdown. In neither case was the popular outrage as widespread as it was this summer. That is likely because those past protests were associated with the Sikh and Muslim communities, which the BJP and its supporters had effectively maligned, playing into and deepening long-standing prejudices. [ Read: Why India is erupting ] By contrast, this summer, many of those demanding the education minister’s resignation came from privileged Hindu families—the very constituents that the prime minister and his party count on for support. The government therefore couldn’t target them with as heavy a hand. The movement culminated in the education minister’s ouster. Right-wing provocateurs and media outlets—aided, in several instances, by police officials and BJP supporters and politicians—singled out Muslim , female , and queer protesters for retaliation. This fall saw the development of a new protest movement in the capital, centering on the denial of a fundamental democratic promise: the right to vote. Since 2025, millions of names have been struck from India’s voter rolls in a revision process that has raised many questions. At stake, Anjali Bhardwaj, an activist, told me, “is the very soul of India’s electoral democracy.” Those agitating against the assault on the franchise repurposed some of the same rallying cries from the summer protests—for instance, “ Jab Jab Modi darta hai, police ko aage karta hai ,” or, “Whenever Modi feels the heat, he sends the police onto the streets.” And the government again turned to repression. Security forces detained thousands of people carrying out flash protests, beating many and confronting others with legal charges. But many citizens now see these tactics less as a show of strength than as an admission of fear. The new movement has not been extinguished, and opposition political parties have come out to show their support. At the same time, other, mostly unrelated protests have erupted or continued in different parts of the country. Since January, workers in at least 10 states have staged a reported 275 strikes. In October alone, tribal residents from a village in Madhya Pradesh lay on mock funeral pyres to protest an $87 billion river-linking project that has displaced them; scores of protesters in Mumbai demanded accountability from a public university over allegations that a student who died by suicide faced caste discrimination there; and students at another public university, in Delhi, successfully agitated for the restoration of a long-defunct students’ union. In Arunachal Pradesh, protesters are resisting a mega-dam project that they say will submerge more than two dozen villages. All of these demonstrations have been met with major police pressure, much of it violent, and persisted in spite of it. “A million mutinies are now finally coming to the fore,” Praveen Donthi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, told me. Intimidating opposition members—“labeling people anti-national, anti-development, all that”—once worked to undermine such movements’ confidence, Donthi said. “That is not working now.” The government has yet to recover from the blow that the summer protests dealt its image, according to Neha, the national president of the left-affiliated All India Students’ Association. (Neha goes by only their first name and uses they/them pronouns.) “The young people who have been part of these protests don’t really believe in the invincible aura of the prime minister at all,” Neha told me. “If anything, he has been acting as a wonderful source of memes and jokes and satire, and that has been the extent of his contribution to the young generation.” T his fall’s protest movement has its roots in an administrative process that began more than a year ago. In June 2025, just before contentious assembly elections in several states, India’s election commission announced that it would revise the country’s voter rolls. India has a process for this, called an Intensive Revision, and it has been done eight times in the past. But this Special Intensive Revision (as it was called) was different. The process was hurried and lacked transparency. Unlike past revisions , the SIR shrank the electorate, and not by a little: It struck 130 million names from the rolls. Many of those deleted had died, moved to another constituency, were registered to multiple polling stations, or could not be found by enumerators. But the effects of the revision could not be explained solely by such cases. For example, the Sabar Institute, a public-policy-research organization, reports that about 70 percent of the 2.7 million voters deleted from electoral rolls in West Bengal after their cases were flagged for adjudication were Muslim, and more than half were women. In one constituency where Muslims made up 20 percent of the population, they accounted for 95 percent of the deletions, Sabir Ahamed, who co-leads the Sabar Institute, told me. A category called “logical discrepancies” excluded voters for inconsistencies in their names across different documents, or for arbitrary criteria such as an insufficient age gap between them and their parents. “What followed was the greatest disruption of the electoral process India has ever seen—barring election boycotts and a rigged election in Kashmir in 1987,” the political scientist Gilles Verniers wrote in June. West Bengal held its state election shortly after the SIR concluded, and the BJP campaigned on the specter of so-called illegal infiltrators from Bangladesh. It won in a landslide. People cut from the electoral rolls have not been disenfranchised only from voting. In West Bengal, the government also denied welfare entitlements to deleted voters, even though the supreme court had earlier clarified that the SIR was not a test of citizenship. And although a process for redress does exist, access to it is inequitable. In at least a few regions, a two-tier system allows enumerators to mark certain people as “VIPs” who can then sidestep the cumbersome process that those from less privileged backgrounds are forced to undergo to restore their name to the rolls. Activists and journalists have raised questions about who decided to undertake this SIR with such haste and why. In the summer of 2025, Bhardwaj, the activist, filed a request for documents that could furnish these details under India’s Right to Information Act. In September, she received a note from the election commission indicating that it had not made the decision to undertake the SIR. But as far as she knew, the commission was the only body constitutionally empowered to do so. If it hadn’t chosen to revise the voter lists, then who had? “This raises a huge question on the constitutionality of the exercise and on the independence of the election commission itself,” she told me. The SIR brought renewed scrutiny to a commission already dogged by allegations of partisanship in favor of the ruling BJP. Then, in a series of investigations published this fall, The Indian Express found that Gyanesh Kumar, the chief election commissioner, had made several SIR decisions unilaterally, in contravention of a requirement that the three-member body make all decisions by consensus. “Gyanesh, it’s done, bro,” became a popular refrain on social media, riffing on a viral tweet from a Bollywood star who had called on protesters to stand down over the summer. A loose coalition began to mobilize, including the Cockroach Janata Party—the pressure group that led the demonstrations in July—together with several left-wing student organizations, the Indian National Congress, and other opposition parties. B y early October, multiple organizations were calling for mass demonstrations to demand Kumar’s resignation and the withdrawal of the SIR. On October 10, when one such protest was to be held, central Delhi became a fortress, its streets lined with police barricades and patrolled by more than 40,000 police officers and paramilitaries. Hotels and guesthouses were directed to not take any fresh bookings; liquor stores were ordered shut. About 50 metro stations were closed and more than 200 trains were canceled, and internet service was suspended around Jantar Mantar, Delhi’s most famous protest site. I walked around the area with a colleague that morning. The quiet was eerie. Loudspeakers on street corners played prerecorded announcements about the orders in place barring “unauthorized gatherings, public speeches, shouting of slogans.” The only people listening were journalists and security personnel. We realized soon after that protesters trying to reach the site were being detained. At one point, we recorded the Delhi police dragging a young man into custody. A flank of officials obstructed our movement and insisted that we needed accreditation from the government press office, although our press cards were prominently displayed. Later that day, another police official in another part of central Delhi directed a group of his female colleagues to push me away when I asked him a question. He called journalists “reel makers” who were “only there to disrupt police work.” The state had learned from its missteps in July. And so the police opted for a quieter strategy this time, picking up protesters before they could congregate and dragging them onto buses. My colleagues and I met several detainees who recounted being assaulted away from the public gaze, often in the vehicles that ferried them to distant holding centers, where they were kept for hours. More than 7,000 people were reportedly detained on October 10 alone. About two dozen journalists were detained that day; the number had nearly doubled by October 11. The pattern continued in the days that followed, as flash protests broke out across the city. Meanwhile authorities forbade the use of Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site. Leaders from the movement, including Neha, were kept in custody for periods ranging from one night to several days. Some were asked to sign documents that would effectively bar them from joining protests. And yet, many citizens continued to show up daily. “I would not even, for a second, count this as the victory of a state. If anything, I would count it as the victory of the people outsmarting the police and the entire system,” Neha told me. I talked with Naureen Sabba, a 26-year-old activist with the Revolutionary Workers’ Party of India who has participated in several protests since she moved to Delhi in 2023. The current movement, she acknowledged, was struggling to expand beyond committed activists and political workers. She pointed to two limiting factors: police dispersal and the loss of Jantar Mantar as a gathering place. “Common people, ordinary students, they are coming,” Sabba insisted. “However, they are coming in scattered groups, because the surveillance and repression of the state are so much that they are not even able to stand together in one place.” [ From the February 2025 issue: Narendra Modi’s populist facade is cracking ] Sabba conjectured that the state’s repression would ultimately backfire. “Think of a spring,” she said. “You can keep pressing it down, pushing it further and further. But there comes a point when, the moment you let go, it recoils with tremendous force. The harder you push it down, the stronger it bounces back.” Donthi, of the International Crisis Group, told me that the protests have had an effect on the Modi government. “The SIR, the process, there is no doubt that it’s problematic, even in the minds of BJP supporters, which has led to a crisis of credibility for Indian democracy itself,” he said. For the moment, however, the movement remains somewhat inchoate and largely confined to the capital. Ajay Gudavarthy, an associate professor of political science at Jawaharlal Nehru University, told me that he had recently traveled to the southern states of Telangana and Tamil Nadu and was struck by the lack of widespread outrage against the SIR. “Those who are in, they are not bothered; and those who are deleted—it’s become an administrative issue,” he said. The demonstrations risk being perceived as a conflict among political forces seeking power, Gudavarthy noted, unless opposition parties can link the SIR deletions to matters of social welfare. I asked Ahamed, from the Sabar Institute, why West Bengal hadn’t seen widespread protests despite the scale of disenfranchisement there. Since the BJP came to power in that state, Islamophobic attacks have risen and the party’s critics have been intimidated into silence, he said. “Even I, after the SIR, couldn’t speak here. Whatever talks and speeches I am giving are outside Bengal. I have started censoring myself, despite being an educated, well-connected researcher.” Ahamed said this was because of his Muslim identity and the fact that the BJP was accusing deleted voters of being infiltrators who should be deported. The issues at hand, Ahamed cautioned, are urgent. If the SIR is not reversed, the next general election, in 2029, might be a foregone conclusion: “We can say who will win.”

items.title: Bagbin warns youth against internet fraud, calls for responsible use of technology
items.description: The Speaker of Parliament, Alban Sumana Kingsford Bagbin, has denounced the rising incidence of cybercrime and internet fraud in Ghana, cautioning the youth to desist from misusing the internet and use technology appropriately. He warned that such practices undermined public trust, tarnished Ghana’s image abroad, and could land offenders in serious trouble with the law. The speaker expressed the concern in a statement delivered on his behalf by the Member of Parliament for Asikuma-Odoben-Brakwa, Kobina Ghansah, at the global launch of the Student Workforce and Innovation Movement (SWIM) project at Asikuma. The SWIM project, a global youth empowerment initiative, seeks to bridge the gap between education and work by equipping students and young people in Africa with contemporary skills and connecting them to paid employment opportunities. Working in partnership with about 50 schools and universities globally as well as several governments, the project aims to remove geographical and technological barriers to give young people equal access to education, professional networks, digital skills, and employment offers, regardless of where they come from. Already, more than 8,000 students across Africa have joined the platform to take part in a raft of courses, including Artificial Intelligence (AI), blockchain, and data science and form friendships with their counterparts abroad. Instead of engaging in cybercrime such as identity theft, online exploitation, and other criminal activities, he urged young people to use technology to build skills, solve problems, and earn legitimate wealth. “It is unfortunate when platforms designed to facilitate learning, communication, and economic advancement are used for cybercrime, internet fraud, identity theft, online exploitation, and other unlawful or immoral activities,” the Speaker noted. “The pursuit of quick and unearned financial gains must never be allowed to replace the values of honesty, hard work, and integrity,” he added. The colourful event was graced by traditional leaders, government officials, business owners, renowned academics, students, the diaspora community, among other stakeholders. Speaker Bagbin underscored the numerous opportunities offered by digital technology, artificial intelligence, social media, e-commerce, and digital financial services, urging the youth to leverage the same to develop businesses, market products, provide professional services, and access international markets. “Technology must be an instrument of empowerment, not exploitation, a platform for enterprise, not criminality, and a force for national development and not societal destruction,” he stressed. He urged strong collaboration among parents, educational institutions, religious bodies, and national institutions to promote digital literacy, ethical conduct, and responsible online behaviour. The Speaker noted that the youth were among Ghana’s greatest national assets, with enormous potential to transform the economy and society through their energy, creativity, ambition, and innovation. In that regard, he said youth empowerment must go beyond acknowledging challenges to creating practical opportunities in education, skills development, employment, entrepreneurship, and public participation. And to the youth, he said they should not only seek employment but also develop innovative solutions, create jobs, and establish sustainable businesses.

items.title: Ghana Petroleum Commission introduces Digital Permit Platform to improve oil sector operations
items.description: The Ghana Petroleum Commission (PC) has introduced a Digital Permit Application Platform to simplify regulatory processes, reduce delays, and improve business operations in Ghana’s upstream petroleum sector. The platform replaces the manual hard-copy application process and is expected to reduce administrative bottlenecks, improve service delivery and strengthen regulatory oversight. Chief Executive Officer of the Commission, Madam Emeafa Hardcastle, announced this at the opening of the Petroleum Commission’s 2026 Local Content Conference and Exhibition in Takoradi in the Western Region. The conference was on the theme: “ Enriching Local Content for Sustainable Growth: Building a Resilient Upstream Sector through Reforms and Partnerships to Spur Competitiveness and Investment “. The initiative formed part of the Commission’s digital transformation agenda to improve the experience of investors and industry operators while creating a more efficient and predictable regulatory environment. Madam Hardcastle said the digital platform went beyond the introduction of technology, as it was intended to facilitate investment and enhance the Commission’s responsiveness to industry needs. The Commission also launched the Local Content Fund to provide financial support to indigenous Ghanaian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in the petroleum industry. She described the Fund as a financial springboard to strengthen local businesses and enhance their capacity to participate competitively in the petroleum value chain. The PC CEO said the Fund’s establishment was the outcome of years of collaboration between the Commission and industry contractors and subcontractors, and urged stakeholders to continue supporting its sustainability. Madam Hardcastle also appealed to the President and the Minister for Finance to allocate funding from the petroleum funds to the Commission to strengthen its institutional and operational capacity. “Given the increasing complexity of the global energy landscape and the need to attract and retain investments in Ghana’s upstream sector, a well-resourced regulator is indispensable,” she said. The Commission plays a critical role in safeguarding the country’s petroleum resources, promoting efficient petroleum operations, facilitating investment and maximising value for Ghana. Ghana has made considerable progress in indigenous participation since the introduction of the Local Content Regulations 13 years ago, and Ghanaian companies have expanded their operations beyond the domestic petroleum industry into other African countries, including Côte d’Ivoire, São Tomé and Angola, and Namibia. She cited the establishment of specialised facilities for chemicals, drilling fluids, cementing mud, steel fabrication, pipe threading and coating as evidence of the growing capabilities of indigenous companies. Meanwhile, workforce localisation had also reached approximately 90 per cent, reflecting progress in developing local expertise and reducing dependence on expatriate personnel. The Petroleum Commission has developed an in-country capabilities and capacities catalogue to showcase the services, facilities and expertise available locally to investors and industry operators and has remained committed to moving local content beyond regulatory compliance towards building globally competitive Ghanaian companies.

items.title: Planet One opens new exploration frontier with offshore Ghana hydrocarbon discovery
items.description: Planet One Oil & Gas has announced the discovery of hydrocarbons at its Nya Gyidie-1X exploration well in the Deepwater Cape Three Points (DWCTP) Block offshore Ghana. Nya Gyidie-1X marks the first successful test of a carbonate reservoir system in Ghana, opening a new geological target beyond the sandstone formations that have underpinned the country’s existing commercial discoveries. The discovery comes as Ghana seeks to accelerate investment and exploration across its upstream petroleum sector. In July 2026, H.E. John Dramani Mahama announced $3.5 billion of new upstream investment commitments. The Government has also identified reserve replacement, increased production and renewed international investment as priorities for the sector. President of the Republic of Ghana, John Mahama said: “The hydrocarbon discovery at the Nya Gyidie-1X well in the Deepwater Cape Three Points Contract Area marks an important milestone for Ghana. It is the country’s first successful test of a Cenomanian–Turonian carbonate play as a primary exploration target. The well also targeted the Albian as a secondary objective. By drilling this well, Planet One and its partners fulfilled an exploration commitment and demonstrated confidence in Ghana and in the direction of our Reset Agenda. That is why I call it a well of faith. Our priority now is to accelerate responsible exploration and put in place the infrastructure Ghana needs to develop its petroleum resources sustainably. Our goal is to turn those resources into jobs and opportunities for Ghanaians and into lasting improvements in people’s lives. I congratulate Planet One and its partners on this achievement.” Sanjeev Mansotra, Founder and Chairman of Planet One Group, added: “The discovery at Nya Gyidie-1X reinforces our confidence in Ghana and the potential of its oil and gas sector, opening new possibilities for future exploration. We have worked closely with the Government of Ghana for many years, and across every project our focus is on the impact it can create for the country. In oil and gas, that means supporting investment, jobs, skills and wider economic value over time. We are grateful to the Government of Ghana, the Ministry of Energy and Green Transition, the Petroleum Commission, Ghana National Petroleum Corporation and GOIL for their continued support and partnership.” Dr. John Jinapor, Minister of Energy and Green Transition, Government of Ghana, said: “This latest hydrocarbon discovery in Ghana marks another significant milestone in our efforts to revitalise the upstream petroleum sector, attract strategic investments, increase production and strengthen our nation’s energy security. Under the leadership of John Dramani Mahama, President of the Republic of Ghana, we remain committed to ensuring that our petroleum resources are responsibly developed to create jobs, accelerate economic growth and deliver lasting prosperity for the people of Ghana. Planet One has been a long-standing partner to the Government across various sectors and this milestone will further strengthen our collaboration going forward.” Mr. Kwame Ntow Amoah, Chief Executive of the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC), said: “The significance of Nya Gyidie-1X goes beyond the hydrocarbons encountered in this well. For the first time in Ghana, we have tested and confirmed hydrocarbons in a carbonate reservoir system, opening up a new geological play for further exploration. At a time when replenishing our reserves and sustaining production growth are national priorities, this is an encouraging development. The next task is to establish the scale and commercial potential of the discovery through rigorous technical evaluation. GNPC looks forward to working with Planet One and GOIL Upstream to build on this result and advance the development and production opportunities it presents for Ghana.” Edward Abambire Bawa, Group Chief Executive Officer of GOIL PLC, said: “The Nya Gyidie-1X hydrocarbon discovery represents an important milestone for Ghana’s upstream petroleum industry and validates GOIL’s strategic decision to participate in exploration through GOIL Upstream Limited. As a Ghanaian company, we are particularly encouraged by the opening of a new exploration frontier and its potential contribution to the country’s long-term energy security. We commend Planet One, the operator, and our partners for this achievement and look forward to the next phase of technical evaluation to establish the discovery’s commercial potential.” Located around 148 kilometres offshore Ghana, Nya Gyidie-1X was drilled in water depths of 2,289 metres, placing it firmly in ultra-deepwater. The well encountered hydrocarbons within carbonate rock between 3,364 and 3,499 metres measured depth along the wellbore, confirming the presence of hydrocarbons in a reservoir type not previously proven in Ghana. The Deepwater Cape Three Points Block, where Nya Gyidie-1X was drilled, covers approximately 1,454 square kilometres offshore Ghana. The block is operated by Planet One in partnership with GOIL Upstream Limited, a subsidiary of GOIL PLC, and the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation. Planet One’s partnership with GOIL Upstream was established in 2023 through Farm-In and Joint Operating Agreements to advance exploration across the block. Planet One’s oil and gas activities in Ghana also extend beyond the Deepwater Cape Three Points Block with the overall portfolio also including other offshore and onshore blocks. Together, these form part of Planet One’s long-term plan to build an exploration and production presence across Ghana’s offshore and onshore petroleum basins.

items.title: Tiris Zemour : un blessé et probablement un mort dans l’attaque au drone d’un camion-citerne dans une zone contrôlée par la Polisario
items.description: Un chauffeur de camion-citerne blessé est arrivé mardi soir au centre médical de la ville de Zouerate, après que son véhicule ait été pris pour cible par un drone dans la matinée dans la région d’Ahfir, située dans la zone contrôlée par le Front Polisario. Selon les informations fournies par le correspondant de « Sahara Media » au Tiris Zemmour, le conducteur, qui a été blessé à plusieurs reprises lors de l’attaque a déclaré croire que son assistant avait trouvé la mort lors de l’attaque, précisant qu’il n’avait pas pu quitter le camion avant qu’il ne soit pris pour cible et que celui-ci avait été réduit en épaves par les tirs. Selon la même source, le camion-citerne venait de la région d’Ahfir et empruntait un itinéraire en direction de la ville d’Atar afin d’éviter les patrouilles douanières de la province du Tiris Zemmour, avant de s’égarer et d’être pris pour cible avant même d’avoir franchi la frontière mauritanienne. Les informations indiquent que certains commerçants se livrent à la contrebande de carburant depuis les zones contrôlées par le Front Polisario, dans le but de le commercialiser dans certaines régions du nord de la Mauritanie, profitant de la différence de prix entre le carburant de contrebande et celui pratiqué sur le marché mauritanien.

items.title: 45-minute downpour floods parts of China Afri Mall, strands commuters in Koforidua
items.description: Parts of the newly established China Afri Mall in Koforidua flooded after about 45 minutes of rain on Tuesday night, stranding commuters and disrupting traffic on surrounding roads. The November 10 downpour inundated key intersections around the commercial facility in the New Juaben South Municipality, renewing concerns about persistent drainage problems. Affected locations included the traffic light intersection near the mall, the stretch around Newlands Hospital and the vicinity of Dadis Bar. Vehicles struggled to navigate the flooded roads, while pedestrians and other commuters faced difficulties crossing the affected areas. According to Citi News, hundreds of commuters and passersby were inconvenienced. Some questioned why drainage problems remained unresolved despite earlier concerns raised by regional authorities. Citi News sources linked the recurring flooding to narrow culverts at the intersection and disagreements over the mall’s management. The Eastern Regional Minister and the Regional Security Council had reportedly directed traditional authorities and the mall’s management to reconstruct the culverts before the facility opened. The work was intended to improve stormwater flow and reduce flood risk. However, the report says the directive was allegedly not implemented before the mall began operations. Some road users criticised the traditional authorities for allegedly failing to comply. They argued that the absence of drainage improvements had contributed to repeated flooding during heavy rainfall. The latest incident has renewed questions about enforcement of the directive and the responsibilities of those tasked with addressing the drainage challenges.

items.title: Dikan partners with dEX, to screen The Eyes of Ghana documentary at DDC26
items.description: In partnership with Dikan, dEX Ghana Foundation will host a special screening of The Eyes of Ghana, the acclaimed documentary directed by Ben Proudfoot, at the National Theatre of Ghana on Friday, November 13, at 6:30 pm. The screening is part of Day 2 of DDC26, the seventh dEX Design Conference. The Eyes of Ghana spotlights 93-year-old Chris Hesse, who served as personal cameraman to Ghana’s founding president, Kwame Nkrumah. Today, Hesse is leading efforts to preserve and restore more than 1,300 reels of historic film footage that capture crucial moments in Ghana’s national history and the broader African liberation movement. The film, from two-time Oscar winner Ben Proudfoot, premiered at the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival. Breakwater Studios and Higher Ground, the production company founded by Barack and Michelle Obama, produced it, and the Obamas are executive producers. American streamer IShowSpeed joined as a producer, his first project in that role, after visiting Ghana on his Speed Does Africa tour. The film played for one night in cinemas across the United States and Canada on 28 October. Dikan has previously brought the film to diverse audiences across the country, and is facilitating this latest screening at DDC26 to highlight the vital connection between sustainability and cultural preservation. It also reflects a belief Dikan and dEX share: that African knowledge and history should be accessible to the creatives who will build on it. The screening sits within Day 2, Planet, which looks at what design decisions leave behind and whether what we build lasts. Hesse’s story is about exactly that: a creative professional who decided a nation’s memory was worth protecting, and spent decades making sure it survived. “Chris Hesse spent a lifetime protecting a part of Ghana’s story. Preserving what matters takes people who care and systems that last, and that is the idea behind everything we build at dEX. “We are proud to partner with Dikan to bring this film to the National Theatre during DDC26, in front of the designers, students and storytellers who will decide what Ghana preserves and creates next,” said Daniel Ampofo, Founder and President of dEX Ghana Foundation. The screening takes place in the evening, after the Day 2 main stage programme. DDC26 passes are available at ticket.dexghana.org.

items.title: Ligue des champions féminine : l'AS FAR bat les Camerounaises de Lekié FF et se qualifie pour la finale
items.description: L'AS FAR s'est qualifiée, mercredi, pour la finale de la Ligue des champions féminine de la CAF (Égypte 2026), en s'imposant face au club camerounais de Lekié Football Filles (1-0), en demi-finale disputée au stade de l'Autorité du canal de Suez, à Ismaïlia. L'unique but de la rencontre a été inscrit par Ghizlane Chebbak à la 48e minute. L'AS FAR avait entamé son parcours dans cette édition par une défaite face au club ougandais de Kawempe Muslim Ladies (2-3), avant de signer deux victoires consécutives contre l'USFAS Bamako du Mali (6-0) et Ampem Darkoa Ladies du Ghana (2-0), lors de la phase de groupes. Dans l'autre demi-finale, prévue plus tard dans la journée, Kawempe Muslim Ladies affrontera les Sud-Africaines de Mamelodi Sundowns pour décrocher le second billet pour la finale. Le vainqueur de cette édition de la Ligue des champions féminine de la CAF se qualifiera pour le deuxième tour des éliminatoires de la Coupe du monde des clubs féminine 2027, où il affrontera en décembre prochain le club nord-coréen de Naegohyang. L'AS FAR et Mamelodi Sundowns sont les clubs les plus titrés de la compétition, avec deux sacres chacun. Le club marocain a remporté le trophée en 2022 et 2025, tandis que la formation sud-africaine s'est imposée en 2021 et 2023. Le TP Mazembe de la République démocratique du Congo a été sacré en 2024. The post Ligue des champions féminine : l'AS FAR bat les Camerounaises de Lekié FF et se qualifie pour la finale appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Burkina : Les acteurs de l’éducation outillés sur la protection des œuvres de l’esprit
items.description: Le Centre national de la propriété intellectuelle (CNPI) a organisé, ce mercredi 11 novembre 2026 à Ouagadougou, un atelier de sensibilisation destiné aux acteurs du monde éducatif. L’objectif est de promouvoir l’enseignement de la propriété intellectuelle dans les établissements d’enseignement général, professionnel, technique et universitaire. Dans un contexte où la protection de la propriété intellectuelle constitue un enjeu majeur pour la valorisation de la créativité et de l’innovation, l’éducation apparaît comme un levier essentiel. Elle permet de transmettre aux jeunes générations les réflexes liés au respect des droits d’auteur et à la protection des œuvres de l’esprit. Lodouba Kohio, représentant du SP/CNPI, expliquant que l'atelier vise en sensibiliser les acteurs du secteur éducatif sur la Propreté intellectuelle C’est dans cette perspective que le Centre national de la propriété intellectuelle (CNPI) a initié cet atelier, qui vise à accroître le nombre d’usagers sensibilisés à la propriété intellectuelle afin de susciter la créativité, l’innovation, le transfert de technologie et l’enseignement de cette discipline à tous les niveaux du système éducatif national. Selon le représentant du secrétaire permanent du CNPI, Lodouba Kohio, il s’agit de passer en revue, avec les acteurs du monde éducatif, la nécessité d’enseigner la propriété intellectuelle à tous les niveaux du système éducatif burkinabè. « L’importance de la propriété intellectuelle n’est plus à démontrer. Cependant, dans notre pays, cette discipline reste relativement méconnue. C’est pourquoi nous avons décidé d’organiser cet atelier afin de faire davantage connaître la propriété intellectuelle, de montrer son importance et de poser les bases de son enseignement dans notre système éducatif », a-t-il déclaré. Dre Rokiatou Zerbo, Participante, attend renforcer ses notions sur la propriété intellectuelle au cours de l'atelier Concrètement, l’atelier vise à susciter la nécessité de définir des curricula de formation et des stratégies de communication en matière de propriété intellectuelle dans les établissements d’enseignement général, professionnel, technique et universitaire. Pour Nicodème Niyonkuru, enseignant permanent en droit privé au Centre de recherche panafricain en management pour le développement (CEPAMAD), cet atelier vise à sortir l’enseignement de la propriété intellectuelle de la simple connaissance générale dans le monde éducatif. « Le constat est que ce domaine reste relativement méconnu et souvent négligé. Il est parfois abordé sous la forme d’un cours de courte durée dans les universités et les différentes institutions d’enseignement supérieur, mais les connaissances acquises ne sont pas suffisamment entretenues. Il manque notamment un suivi permettant de mieux faire comprendre les réalités et les retombées de la propriété intellectuelle. L’organisation d’un atelier de ce genre contribue donc à faire connaître davantage cette discipline », a-t-il fait savoir. S’exprimant en tant que participante, la Dre Rokiatou Zerbo a affiché son intention de renforcer ses connaissances en matière de propriété intellectuelle grâce à cet atelier, car celle-ci revêt une importance particulière pour le développement socio-économique de chaque nation. « Elle permet de valoriser les différents résultats de recherche que nous produisons au niveau de nos instituts. À travers cet atelier, nous espérons mieux connaître les procédures permettant de protéger les résultats de nos recherches, afin de faciliter leur transfert vers le secteur privé. Celui-ci pourra ensuite les reproduire et les mettre à la disposition de la population », a-t-elle signifié. Un aperçu du public Pour information, le CNPI est une structure de mission du ministère chargé de l’Industrie, du Commerce et de l’Artisanat. Il assure les fonctions de l’Association nationale de liaison avec l’Organisation africaine de la propriété intellectuelle (OAPI) et constitue la porte d’entrée de la propriété intellectuelle au Burkina Faso. Son rôle consiste à promouvoir la propriété intellectuelle sur le territoire national et à accompagner les créateurs dans les démarches de protection de leurs créations auprès de l’OAPI. Cet atelier réunit environ une trentaine de personnes. Jean-François SOMÉ Minute.bf
