items.title: The Left’s Election Denial
items.description: B ernie Sanders and his acolytes have spent the past decade insisting that Democrats would command national majorities if only they embraced his left-wing policies. After last week’s election, the movement claimed vindication. The results proved that “we can win over millions of Republicans and independents who are struggling economically if we focus on the issues that are important,” Sanders told Politico . In reality, the results point in the opposite direction. Almost every Democratic Senate nominee gained a higher vote share in their state than Kamala Harris did two years earlier, but the five left-wing candidates backed by Sanders accounted for the four smallest swings in contested races. The one candidate who underperformed Harris, Troy Jackson in Maine, was a Sanders-backed progressive. By the same measure, moderate Democrats in the House also outperformed progressives. Newcomers such as incoming Senators Josh Turek of Iowa and Annie Andrews of South Carolina came out against gender-affirming surgery for minors and allowing transgender female athletes to compete in girls’ sports—positions that did grave damage to Harris. Both of them, along with James Talarico in Texas and Adam Hamilton in Kansas, rejected Medicare for All. Ballot referenda in multiple states—banning the government from giving preferential treatment on the basis of race and other factors, rejecting a wealth tax —confirmed that the public’s rejection of the GOP did not entail a full embrace of the Democratic Party’s left wing. The party’s most impressive victories, compared with the recent election outcomes in historically purple states, came from mainstream or moderate candidates: Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia (who won by 18 points), Senator-Elect Roy Cooper of North Carolina (19.6), and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro (21.5 points). Although every contest has unique circumstances, and no single result can be reduced to a simple test of ideology, the overall pattern is unmistakable. [ Jonathan Chait: Mamdani is the centrist we’ve been waiting for ] Because the whole party blew the doors out, many of its left-wing candidates won anyway. But not all of them. In Maine, the moderate Representative Jared Golden retired in the face of a progressive primary challenger. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee—the dreaded party establishment—had hoped to retain the seat by nominating a mainstream Democrat. Instead, Matt Dunlap, a progressive supporter of Medicare for All backed by Sanders’s organization Our Revolution, won the nomination. The left-wing American Prospect , in an article headlined “The New Majority Makers,” praised Dunlap as “a working-class northern Mainer” who is “committed to economic populism.” Dunlap lost, turning what had been the reddest district held by a Democrat into the bluest district held by a Republican. If the election was a test of whether Americans like Sanders’s message more or less than the standard Democratic message, the answer was clear: They like it less. Unfortunately, true believers deny this reality. When Democrats are enjoying tidal waves of public support, like they did in last week’s election, the cost of this denial is small. Under more regular political circumstances, such as the closely balanced elections that have typically occurred this century, finding an acceptable way to compromise with public opinion is often the difference between winning and losing elections. T he question of whether individual candidates are helped or harmed by moving toward the center has been studied extensively and has a firm answer. The data measuring the effect of moderation on winning elections, somewhat like the data confirming anthropogenic global warming, can be noisy and messy but, in the general sweep of things, generally point in one direction : All things being equal, congressional candidates who advocate more ideologically extreme positions tend to do worse. As voters have polarized, penalties for extremism seem to have shrunk , but they haven’t disappeared . Newer models confirm that moderate candidates tend to overperform the partisan composition of their district, but extreme candidates underperform it. Both parties have a contingent of vocal activists who deny that any such penalty for extremism exists. The arguments used by progressive activists roughly mirror those used by conservative activists: The voters in their hearts agree with our values, and the key to winning is to mobilize this hidden majority by ignoring the elitists in our party who, for their own selfish reasons, are intent on foisting wishy-washy centrists upon the electorate . The progressive movement has a small array of academic and quasi-academic experts who bolster the arguments used by their activists. Yet if you pay careful attention to the claims made by the wonks, they do not line up with the arguments put forward by the activists. The progressive wonks tend to make relatively modest claims. “A growing body of research now demonstrates that the moderation advantage has largely disappeared,” the political scientists Adam Bonica and Jake Grumbach wrote in Boston Review in February. In an essay last year, G. Elliott Morris, a statistician and Substack writer popular with the left, wrote , “While there used to be a large premium for ideological moderation, it has decreased markedly over the last 25 years.” They are not saying that left-wing candidates enjoy advantages, or even that the electoral benefits of moderation are zero—only that they are smaller than they used to be. Morris, for example, estimates that strategic moderation in 2024 would have increased any given House candidate’s margin by two to three points, a smaller effect than some other recent studies have found. Morris titled his essay “Moderation Is Not a Silver Bullet.” This is technically accurate—moderation would not solve every problem the Democratic Party has—but a two-and-a-half-point swing is larger than the margin that decided five of the past seven presidential elections. By contrast, the activists who dispute the electoral benefit to moderation seem drawn to sweeping assertions that extreme ideology is no burden whatsoever. “The results show that there is no electoral penalty for being a progressive,” Representative Ro Khanna of California told The New York Times after last week’s election. “The stale talking points of the establishment, which lost twice to Trump, about who they deem electable or not electable is totally out the window.” Others go even further, insisting that advocating left-wing politics confers an insurmountable advantage. “Bernie would have won in a landslide,” Shawn Fain, head of the United Automobile Workers union, told the columnist Michelle Goldberg in August, repeating an oft-made progressive assertion about the 2016 election. Morris relentlessly trolls advocates of moderation on social media as untrustworthy ideologues. Grumbach has repeatedly argued that the correct conclusion is to “reject the false aura of scientific certainty” around the benefits of moderation. The message, like that of climate-science skeptics, is that the data are hopelessly muddled and no firm conclusions can be drawn. This allows their allies to simultaneously argue that Sanders-style populism is the one true path to political success and, when faced with the mountain of data refuting this, that there’s no way to tell. P rogressives have more or less succeeded in shaping news coverage of this debate. The morning after the election, Politico ran one story headlined “Progressive Victories Are Now Too Loud to Dismiss,” followed by another the next day, headlined: “Bernie Sanders Lost the Fight in 2016. A Decade Later, He Won the War.” The New York Times followed up with an article covering the debate in studiously neutral terms: “For centrists, the results demonstrate that the best way to flip conservative strongholds where their party has long struggled is through embracing moderate candidates and positions that appeal to a broader array of voters. Progressives argue that the victories in Maine and Michigan show that left-wing populists can energize the party’s liberal base and win back some of the working-class voters who had flocked to President Trump.” A reader would not have guessed that the empirical debate is over how much of an advantage moderates have in winning elections, not which posture is more advantageous. Another Times news story on the subject gives the left-wing interpretation even more credulous treatment. In the article, the arguments put forward by the left provide a revealing specimen of its inability to accept evidence that its ideas can hurt candidates who endorse them. The story conveys a progressive complaint that “centrists said they would lose in the fall and cost the party control of Congress,” only to move the goalposts. The story does not cite a single example of a centrist having done this. In fact, before the election, moderate Democratic groups such as Third Way were projecting that the entire party would do well, that moderates would overperform baseline partisanship, and that progressive candidates would underperform. That is precisely what happened. The article asserts that Abdul El-Sayed, the left-wing senator-elect in Michigan, “underperformed Jocelyn Benson, now the Democratic governor-elect in Michigan, by only a small margin.” Oddly, the article omits the gap between Benson’s margin and El-Sayed’s: 3.9 percentage points, which, in a normal election year in a state like Michigan, could easily make the difference between winning and losing. [ Sarah Longwell: Voters have a message for Democrats ] Most amazing, the story excuses Jackson’s narrow victory by noting that he “was facing Senator Susan Collins, perhaps the most formidable Republican incumbent anywhere on the map.” Of course Collins is the most formidable Republican. The reason is that she has built a reputation as a moderate, the value of which is the entire issue of contention. Defeating a moderate like Susan Collins is hard is a bizarre way to dispute the notion that moderation confers a political advantage. That such incoherent reasoning now appears unrebutted in the paper of record is a disturbing indicator of its influence on mainstream thinking. After the 2018 elections led to a handful of left-wing Democrats winning in deep-blue districts, the progressive narrative swept through the news media. Nearly the entire Democratic presidential field except Joe Biden raced leftward on policy. If Democrats enjoy another wave election in 2028, that might not hurt them. If conditions normalize, however, an inability to acknowledge the trade-off between left-wing purity and electoral success could bring a painful price. This does not mean that progressives cannot win elections—with favorable enough circumstances, many of them obviously can. And it certainly doesn’t mean that Democrats always have to nominate the most electable moderates over left-wingers who have a higher risk of losing. Political parties often have to weigh popularity against commitment to their policy goals. It does mean, however, that Democrats should recognize that the easy solutions the progressive insurgency has proposed over the past decade—that left-wing economic policy is so popular that the party does not need to compromise on any social policies—remains a fantasy.

items.title: The Perverse Reason Health-Care Costs Are About to Surge
items.description: If 2026 was the year of gas prices, 2027 will be the year of health-insurance premiums. The cost of employer-provided health coverage—the kind that 160 million Americans get—is expected to rise by as much as 11 percent, roughly double the average annual increase over the past decade. “These are the highest numbers we’ve ever seen,” Ellen Kelsay, the president and CEO of the Business Group on Health, an organization that lobbies on behalf of large employers, told me. “And the current projections are likely an understatement.” Much of the increase will be passed on to employees—either directly, in the form of higher premiums, co-pays, and deductibles, or indirectly, in the form of reduced benefits, smaller raises, and slower hiring. The biggest reason this is all happening is deeply perverse: A law designed to end surprise medical billing has turned into a tool for squeezing even more money out of insurers and raising the cost of care for everyone else. The upcoming spike is a case of a bad situation getting worse. Over the past decade, the cost of employer-sponsored health insurance has increased by 50 percent, much higher than overall inflation. A 2026 KFF survey found that the average yearly cost for a family of four was about $28,300, of which employees paid about $7,400. The reasons for this trend are well-documented: an aging workforce in need of more care, an increase in the prevalence of chronic illness, and a dramatic consolidation of the hospital sector. Next year’s projected increase is being driven by three additional factors. The first is the mass adoption of GLP-1s. The share of Americans using these drugs for weight loss nearly quadrupled from 2024 to 2026. Even after discounts and rebates, the estimated cost per patient is about $7,000 to $9,000 a year. Projections from Marsh, a health-care-consulting firm, imply that GLP-1s will account for up to a quarter of next year’s rise in costs compared to the preexisting trend. The second explanation appears to be AI. Over the past few years, providers have begun adopting AI tools that record and transcribe their meetings with patients. The ostensible justification for these systems is to give the doctor more time talking with the patient and less time filling out paperwork. But these products are designed to hunt for and maximize revenue from moments during an appointment that a doctor ordinarily might not bill for, such as noting a patient’s chronic disease during a routine checkup. [ Jenisha Watts: The impossible predicament of the uninsured ] The companies that make these tools are very open about this purpose. Ambience Healthcare urges doctors to use its products to “protect your bottom line with stronger documentation” and “capture every dollar earned—automatically.” Another company, Suki, claims that its AI scribes generate up to $6,566 in revenue per clinician per year by increasing the share of patient visits classified at more complex billing rates. Analyses from Marsh and the Business Group on Health imply that AI coding inflation will explain up to a quarter of next year’s extra health-insurance inflation. The final and likely largest explanation for the upcoming cost spike is also the most surprising—and infuriating. Before 2022, if a patient visited an in-network hospital but received care from an out-of-network provider, their insurance would typically cover only the in-network rate, and the patient would receive an unexpected bill for the remaining amount. The No Surprises Act, which was passed in 2020 and came into effect two years later, made this practice illegal. The law imposed a seemingly simple solution: Patients in these situations would be responsible for only their portion of the in-network cost. On the back end, however, the reform was more complicated. The out-of-network provider and insurer would be required to negotiate on any further payment among themselves. If the two sides couldn’t come to an agreement, they would enter a process known as independent dispute resolution, or IDR, in which both parties would submit their desired payment amount to a third-party arbitrator. Government agencies estimated that the law would give rise to only about 17,000 of these disputes a year, given that both sides would likely want to avoid the risk of having to accept the other’s number. They were wrong. After the law took effect, health-care providers began submitting far more arbitration requests than expected, often demanding much higher compensation than any insurer would be willing to pay. The trend began slowly in 2022 and increased with each passing year. In 2025, providers filed 2.6 million disputes. (Technically, either side can initiate arbitration, but in practice, arbitration happens only once an insurer refuses to pay the amount requested, meaning that providers are the ones triggering the process more than 99 percent of the time.) According to a report from Georgetown University’s Center on Health Insurance Reforms, half of those disputes originated from just two provider practices: Radiology Partners, which is majority-owned by private equity and venture capital, and TeamHealth, which is owned by the private-equity giant Blackstone. Another 27 percent came from HaloMD, a company that, as Stat has reported , was founded in 2022 specifically to help providers earn as much money as possible from IDR disputes. “This really isn’t about your average doctor trying to get a fair rate,” Jack Hoadley, a professor emeritus at Georgetown who co-authored the aforementioned report, told me. “It’s an active strategy by a few companies with a lot of money trying to game the system.” The volume of claims was 50 percent higher in the first half of 2026 than in the same period a year earlier, and experts expect it to rise even faster next year. The entities taking advantage of the IDR process tend to point the finger at insurance companies. “The health insurance lobby’s false narrative that the IDR process has increased medical spending is not supported by the data,” a spokesperson for HaloMD told me in an email. A spokesperson for TeamHealth wrote to me, “TeamHealth supports the No Surprises Act and its independent dispute resolution process because it works. Patients are protected from surprise medical bills, and providers have an essential path to challenge insurers’ attempts to deny, delay, or lower fair reimbursement for the life-saving care we provide.” And Radiology Partners sent me a document arguing, “Congress thoughtfully designed the No Surprises Act to protect patients from surprise medical bills while preserving sustainable payment rates that protect patient access to care. Unfortunately, some insurers have disrupted that goal.” [ Annie Lowrey: Annoying people to death ] Since the law was enacted, providers have won about 85 percent of submitted disputes. In 2025, the median award they earned was more than four times the typical in-network cost for the service in question. (HaloMD notes on its website that it has a win rate of more than 88 percent and that the average reward is more than five times the qualifying payment amount.) In one case reviewed by The New York Times , a Dallas surgeon who had accepted a patient’s insurance was paid $1,843 for a prostate-removal operation; the surgeon’s assistant, who had not accepted the insurance, went through arbitration and made $50,456 for the same procedure. The Times investigation also revealed that a single plastic-surgery practice had submitted more than 6,000 arbitration claims, which had earned his practice as much as $440,000 for a single breast-reduction surgery. (The typical cost for breast-reduction surgery in the United States ranges from $9,000 to $15,000.) Some providers argue that they win so often because insurance companies refuse to negotiate in good faith. An analysis by a group of physicians’ lobbies points out that in 8 percent of IDR disputes, insurers have submitted claims of $1 or less, and in about 25 percent of cases, the insurer didn’t submit a counter at all, resulting in an automatic win for the provider. But in a forthcoming analysis, Hoadley finds that 90 percent of insurer offers are either at or above the qualifying payment amount. When insurers don’t submit their own claim, that’s likely because they can’t keep up with the volume of submissions. An executive at the Health Care Service Corporation, a large health-insurance plan, recently told a conference audience that his company currently had “well over 400 people just working IDR disputes.” Several recent papers by health-policy scholars offer a compelling explanation for why providers so consistently win such huge awards: The arbitrators have strong financial incentives to rule in their favor. IDR arbitrators are not public servants working at a federal agency; they are employees of a handful of for-profit companies and nonprofit organizations that are compensated based on the number of claims they process. This creates perverse incentives. The arbitrators get paid only if providers submit cases, and providers will be more likely to submit cases if they expect to win. In many cases, providers get to choose which arbitration company will hear their case. “The more these arbitrators rule on behalf of providers, the more money they ultimately make,” Christopher Whaley, a health economist at Brown University, told me. “So what you end up with is a competition between arbitrators to be the most provider-friendly.” The arbitration organizations that side most often with providers indeed turn out to receive the most submissions. Hoadley and his co-author, Kennah Watts, point out that in the first half of 2024, the arbitration company that received the most cases decided more than 90 percent of them in favor of providers; the entity with the least cases submitted, less than 1 percent of the total, decided in favor of providers only a third of the time. (Making matters even more ethically dubious, some private-equity firms have invested in both the arbitration companies that hear claims and the practices submitting the claims, according to the Private Equity Stakeholder Project.) The costs of this unintended consequence are enormous. The New York Department of Civil Service, for example, has incurred more than $200 million in additional claim payments from IDR for the state-employee health plan, which the agency described as “a primary contributor to the nearly 10 percent increase in premium rates” in 2025. At the national level, Hoadley and Watts estimate that the combination of administrative costs and payments above the in-network rate added up to a total cost of about $1.6 billion a year from 2022 to 2024. In 2025, that number spiked to $16.6 billion. Experts expect it to be even higher in 2027 as more and more providers take advantage of a system that is basically handing out money. Projections by consulting firms imply that this could account for 25 to 40 percent of the extra rise in employer health-insurance costs next year. “I don’t think we’ve seen the worst of it yet—not even close,” Whaley told me. “This is a tidal wave that could totally wipe out health-care affordability if it isn’t fixed.” [ Toluse Olorunnipa: ‘We are looking at a massive crisis’ ] Employers are already scrambling to deal with these rising costs. Disney recently announced that it would be dropping health coverage for working spouses with access to their own coverage next year. Starbucks is one of several major companies that are ending their coverage of GLP-1s for weight loss. Deloitte is rolling back its parental-leave and IVF-funding benefits for certain employees. But these tactics will go only so far. Higher premiums appear inevitable. According to KFF, employee premiums for family coverage increased by 9 percent in 2026, the fastest rate since 2010. If current projections are correct, that figure will be even higher next year, and likely will be accompanied by higher deductibles and co-pays. The good news is that, unlike structural factors driving up health-care costs over the long term, the unintended consequences of the No Surprises Act should be susceptible to a legislative fix. (One House bill , for example, would scrap the IDR process and tie compensation to existing in-network rates.) The cost-of-living crisis in America is the result of a complex set of factors that will not all be easy to reverse. At the very least, Congress should start by solving the problems of its own making.

items.title: ‘Make Politics Boring Again’
items.description: I f you’re a Democrat looking for razzle-dazzle in your politicians, Representative Jake Auchincloss might disappoint you. During an October swing through South Carolina, Auchincloss told a group of military veterans, “I think we have to make politics boring again,” drawing more nods and chuckles than whoops of approval. At times the 38-year-old Auchincloss, young and ambitious though he is, seems to embody the change that he seeks in the world. Spend enough time with him, as I did over the past several months, and you’ll learn more than you ever wanted to know about the evils of “cost disease” (and why inflation is worst in industries such as health care and education), the travails of family-owned pharmacies, and the importance of tutoring in public schools. You’ll be bombarded by an impressive and occasionally overwhelming array of statistics and factoids. (Did you know that Auchincloss’s highly engaged constituents in Massachusetts send him three times as much mail as in the average congressional district? I do now.) You might even start talking like you received a business degree from MIT, where taxes are called levies and everything is either “upstream” of this or “downstream” of that. Most of all, you will discover that Auchincloss has plenty of serious ideas about how the Democratic Party can earn back the trust of voters and use government to improve the lives of Americans. What he does not have right now is an obvious place to go with all of them. “The liberals need a new lion,” Auchincloss told me. Lest we get ahead of ourselves: Auchincloss will not be that lion—at least not yet. He is not running for president; he’s not even all that popular within his own caucus, having irritated colleagues with his willingness to criticize his party. But Auchincloss, who was registered as a Republican not that long ago, wants to have a say in who gets the Democratic presidential nomination and the platform that he or she campaigns on. To that end, he and the group he chairs, Majority Democrats, have summoned the many party leaders who are eyeing White House bids to Denver on Thursday for a postelection conference appropriately titled What’s Next. Auchincloss has found plenty to criticize in a party that lost two elections to Donald Trump, and even as it became clear that Democrats would do well last week, he did not view the elections as evidence that the party had repaired a damaged brand. “There’s not a line out the door for the Democratic Party,” he said. He wants prospective candidates to speak to a party base that he defined as “a morally serious, market-oriented, exhausted majority of Americans who feel increasingly orphaned by both parties.” After Democrats did better than just about anyone—not least Auchincloss—expected, I asked him whether he wished to revise his assessment. He said he did not, although he admitted that, at least at the polls, “there probably was a line out the door for Democrats on Tuesday.” [ Read: The simple message that produced a Democratic landslide ] Auchincloss’s pitch for 2028 aspirants to make the trip to his Denver confab was hardly subtle, and even a bit presumptuous coming from a third-term House member with few concrete accomplishments to his name: One press release quoted Auchincloss as saying the event was an opportunity “to debate a vision for the Democratic Party. Politicians who believe they have that vision should be on that stage.” A significant number of high-profile Democrats answered his call, among them Pete Buttigieg , Josh Shapiro , Raphael Warnock, and Cory Booker . Auchincloss has his own vision for “a new American dream,” one that weaves together plans to help young people, families, and retirees, and is concise enough to fit in a 30-second ad, if not on a bumper sticker. Democrats, he said, should ensure that people have “an excellent education by 18 years old, a home of your own by 30, and a dignified retirement by 65.” He’s trying to find a path for liberals between the ascendant populist left on one side and the sclerotic party establishment on the other. “The core question I get is, like, Jake, what else is there? ” he said. “That is my work.” A uchincloss does not rattle easily. He’s a frequent guest on Fox News and a regular visitor to American Legion halls in his district, where he enjoys arguing over politics with older and mostly conservative war veterans who believe that the Democratic Party is full of criminal-coddling Communists. (Sample question: “Are you a member of DSA?”) Auchincloss does not think highly of the many Democrats who curse in public, and aides tell me he doesn’t even do so in private. That’s not the only fad in Democratic politics that annoys Auchincloss. Graham Platner was another. Auchincloss was dismissive of the progressive Maine oyster farmer long before a sexual-assault allegation forced Platner to drop his bid for Senate in July. (Platner denied the allegation.) Auchincloss called on Platner to withdraw soon after it was revealed that he had a tattoo resembling a Nazi-era Totenkopf . Platner survived that and other scandals, but even when he faced only token opposition in the Democratic primary, Auchincloss publicly urged Mainers to vote for someone else. The comments sparked a brief firestorm, as Platner backers accused Auchincloss of essentially endorsing Senator Susan Collins in a race that could have preserved a Republican majority. (Auchincloss then made clear that he was not backing Collins, who lost her race to Troy Jackson last week.) “Character matters,” Auchincloss said. “Republicans decided it doesn’t,” he continued, citing Trump and the scandal-plagued Ken Paxton, who lost a Texas U.S. Senate race, as examples. The Democrats who triumphed last week, he said, validated that belief. [ Read: How Texas turned blue ] Yet Auchincloss’s visceral distaste for Platner extends beyond scandals and leads into a debate that could complicate his own political future. Democrats gravitated toward Platner’s candidacy because they thought that he offered voters the authenticity they craved—a gruff but charismatic working-class populist, and a first-time candidate for office. In their view, that he had slipped up in the past—some non-PC Reddit posts, a problematic tattoo—made him only more real and relatable. Auchincloss believes that was all wrong, and not just because Platner’s story was not as bootstrap as his campaign made it seem. Some of the candidates whom Majority Democrats—along with its allied organization, the Bench—helped to recruit this year cut a similar profile. They came from working-class backgrounds and were new to elective politics. But when I asked Auchincloss about the voters’ apparent desire for candidates who didn’t look like they were born in a suit and hadn’t spent years preparing to run for office, he became as animated as I’d ever seen him. “I find that to be so condescending to the working class,” Auchincloss replied, “this snickering elitist attitude that somehow if you’re going to appeal to the working class, you need a lot of tattoos and you need to be a bigot.” “Bigotry right now in the Democratic Party is not with the working class,” he continued. “It is in faculty lounges in my alma mater after October 7, for example.” (Auchincloss received an undergraduate degree from Harvard.) “I just find that whole vein so grating,” he said. A uchincloss did not enter the world, so far as I could discern, wearing a suit and tie. But he is the first to acknowledge that he has led a privileged life. (“I was born on easy street,” he said.) His father, Hugh Auchincloss Jr., is a prominent immunologist who succeeded Anthony Fauci to become the acting director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases during the Biden administration. His mother, Laurie Glimcher, for years led the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston. The branches of Auchincloss’s family tree include Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis and Gore Vidal. The route that took Auchincloss to Congress by the age of 32—elite schools, military service, a campaign partially funded by his parents—was smooth and almost Kennedy-esque. (The previous representative of Massachusetts’s Fourth District was, in fact, Joe Kennedy III.) Growing up in the Boston suburbs, Auchincloss was “very interested in U.S. history and very patriotic,” a close friend since childhood, Dani Kirsztajn, told me. Joining the Marine Corps in the early 2010s, when the nation was mired in unpopular wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, was not a typical move for a Harvard graduate from a wealthy New England family. Auchincloss drew inspiration from his grandfather on his mother’s side, a son of Russian Jewish immigrants who enlisted in the Marines during World War II. The military sent his grandfather to college instead of combat, and he ended up pioneering the development of prosthetic limbs. But Auchincloss also told me that in joining the Marines, he had simply “wanted to do something challenging.” It felt to him “like the hardest path I could choose at that point.” Auchincloss was deployed to Afghanistan and then to Panama, ultimately earning a promotion to major. After returning home in 2014, he worked for the campaign of Charlie Baker, a moderate Republican who became Massachusetts governor. Auchincloss even registered as a Republican so that he could vote for Baker at the party convention. While getting his MBA, Auchincloss won a seat on Newton’s city council and then ran for Kennedy’s House seat in 2020, which Kennedy had vacated to mount an ill-fated bid for Senate. Auchincloss’s opponents complained about his GOP past (he called himself an “Obama-Baker voter”). Reporters dredged up old social-media posts in which he seemed to defend the burning of the Quran and criticized the city of Cambridge for “taking PC too far” by changing the name of Columbus Day to Indigenous Peoples’ Day. (Auchincloss has come around on Indigenous Peoples’ Day and said that his Quran comment was “a stupid remark by a snarky 22-year-old.”) [ Read: Pete Buttigieg in the wilderness ] Auchincloss won the crowded 2020 primary by just over 2,000 votes and has not had a difficult election since. When he arrived in Washington, he found a roommate in Representative Jared Golden of Maine, another Marine Corps veteran with a young family in the Democratic caucus. The two quickly became friends, often debating issues such as trade policy over their morning coffee. “I like that he’s a nerdy policy wonk,” Golden told me. “But then he’s also pretty savvy when it comes to the politics” of an issue. During Auchincloss’s first years in Congress, Golden said, he was not afraid to butt heads with committee chairs and other older Democrats who did not take kindly to a young, new member pushing his way into negotiations over major legislation. “There’s no doubt that it’s ruffled some feathers,” Golden said. Auchincloss is earnest almost to a fault. A few people described him to me as self-serious and even cutthroat, occasionally acting, in the words of one Democrat, “like he was playing a character on House of Cards .” It might not help that, but for the patch of thinning hair at the front of his head, Auchincloss could pass for a teenager. A different Democrat compared him unfavorably to Representative Seth Moulton, another ambitious and relatively young military veteran who clashed with progressives in Massachusetts. “Moulton was the least-popular member of the Massachusetts delegation,” this Democrat told me, “until Jake showed up.” When I repeated that to Auchincloss, he replied: “Politics is a brass-knuckle business. I’m happy that people who support me are willing to go on the record, and the people who don’t want to stay on background.” A uchincloss can be hard to place on the traditional political spectrum, which he sees as a point of pride. When I was speaking with one of his close House allies, Representative Hillary Scholten of Michigan, she casually referred to him as a centrist. And when you hear Auchincloss criticize Democrats for backing “catastrophic” school closures during the pandemic, ignoring voter concerns about the porous southern border, or downplaying the rise in crime during the same period, he sounds like he’s aiming for the political middle. He told me, for example, that he still supports Charlie Baker, who left office in 2023. But the policies that Auchincloss is passionate about are not necessarily moderate. He’s in favor of sharply increasing taxes on inheritance, and he said he’s not opposed in principle to a wealth tax—a proposal long associated with the senior senator in his home state, Elizabeth Warren. Auchincloss has denounced the big social-media companies for “attention-fracking our youth.” He wants to tax them, too, and use the money to pay for tutoring every child in America as a way of closing gaps in literacy and math. (Auchincloss said that the only social-media site he regularly uses is LinkedIn.) Auchincloss has become perhaps the biggest congressional champion of independent pharmacies, which are fighting to survive against behemoths such as CVS, Walgreens, Amazon, and the big insurers. He’s introduced several bills aimed at helping family pharmacies and lowering drug prices, building a coalition that has included the fiercely partisan GOP chair of the House Oversight Committee, Representative James Comer of Kentucky, and the far-left Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan. “It’s quite simply small business versus big insurance,” Auchincloss told a group of mostly small-town pharmacists that he had convened in South Carolina. He talked to them about the difference between an economy that works “like Legos,” which rewards diligence and rule following, instead of like Monopoly, in which dominant players hoard property and take over the game. “You,” he told the pharmacists, “are at the vanguard of an economy that works like Legos, the kind of economy that we want to build.” [ Read: The unlikeliest Democratic win of all ] Yet if Auchincloss’s anti-monopoly stance might make Bernie Sanders proud, he’s not sold on the most far-reaching progressive priorities . I struggled to pin him down, for example, on Medicare for All. Majority Democrats is backing a narrower plan that would create a public option for health insurance but stop short of single-payer health care. Auchincloss wants to have a different debate altogether. Democrats, he told me, too often want to argue about who pays the bill for health care—patients, insurers, the government—instead of trying to lower the bill itself. “This is a really critical area of differentiation between my wing and the left,” he said. “What I reject is the concept that Medicare for All is the big idea, and being against Medicare for All is a smaller idea. The big idea from Americans is lower premiums—lower the bill for health care.” His argument notwithstanding, some progressives are likely to make support for Medicare for All a litmus test for Democrats aspiring to party leadership, whether in Congress or the White House. “I close no doors on solutions,” Auchincloss said of Medicare for All when I pressed him again, “but my focus is on the things that we can do right now to lower prices.” Such hedging is one reason progressives remain suspicious of Auchincloss and Majority Democrats, which draws funding from wealthy donors who are opposed to some of the expensive, transformational proposals that progressives run on. “Nothing against Jake Auchincloss, but he does not have the standing or reputation to be telling the Democratic Party to trim its sails at this moment when people are angry and want big solutions,” Adam Green, a co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, told me. Majority Democrats and the Bench helped recruit and fund some of the midterm campaign’s breakout stars, including James Talarico and Bobby Pulido in Texas and Adam Hamilton in Kansas. They did suffer defeats; some of their candidates lost primary races to more progressive Democrats who went on to prevail in the general election. “Voters agreed with us in opposing Trump,” Auchincloss told me after the election. “They are still waiting to be enlisted in what we are for , and that project remains in front of us.” In the near term, he said, Democrats should use their new majorities in Congress to “end the war, repeal the tariffs, and prosecute Pete Hegseth,” before turning to “sensible, fast-acting fixes” on health care and immigration. “We got a permission slip on Election Day,” Auchincloss said, “and we should read it as a chance to show voters that we get it.” Few people who know Auchincloss doubt that his ambitions extend well beyond a House seat in Massachusetts. He considered challenging Senator Ed Markey this year but passed on the race—a decision that looks smart, considering the 80-year-old incumbent defeated Moulton in a primary by nearly 30 points. Massachusetts Democrats expect Auchincloss to run for governor in 2030, but that election is a long way off, and he’d likely have plenty of competition within the party. The size and breadth of the Democrats’ House majority could open up new opportunities for him to advance in Congress, or he could contend for a Cabinet post should the party retake the presidency in 2028. For now, Auchincloss insists that he just wants to have a voice, and to help bring his party fully back to power. But at a moment when the party is teeming with Democrats who want to lead it, even that dream might be a lot to ask.

items.title: What my mother’s death in Lahore taught me about patient care
items.description: I never imagined that taking my mother to hospital would end with her death. On 22 January 2026, my 83-year-old mother was admitted to a private hospital in Lahore after suffering burns in a household accident. We took her there because we believed she would receive appropriate medical treatment, careful monitoring and compassionate care. Like most families, we placed our trust in the doctors, nurses and hospital system. She did not survive. I recognise that medicine is complex, that elderly patients with serious injuries can deteriorate despite the best possible treatment, and that not every death is preventable. But I was with my mother throughout much of her 26-day admission and witnessed the treatment, her deterioration and the way our family struggled to communicate with the team. I share here the questions about care she received in the hope that it may help other families. My mother’s hospitalisation In January, my mother accidentally stood too close to a gas heater and her clothes caught fire. Fortunately, the fire was extinguished within approximately a minute, and she did not suffer an inhalation injury. She sustained second-degree burns to her legs and was admitted to the burns unit and treated by a consultant, who headed it. Initially, she received topical treatment, and her wounds were scrubbed and dressed daily. The wound-scrubbing process was extremely painful. She would scream during some procedures and would be physically and emotionally exhausted afterwards. She was given opioid and non-opioid medications at different times for the pain. As her daughter and carer, I repeatedly questioned whether her pain-management plan was appropriate given her age, her condition and her changing medical status. I was concerned about the risks and benefits of the medication being used, but I did not feel that my questions were adequately explained or addressed. Antibiotics and deterioration As her wounds developed signs of infection, my mother was treated with intravenous antibiotics. During the first two weeks, she received two courses but developed significant problems, including painful blisters in her mouth, a marked fall in haemoglobin and increasing difficulty eating. I cannot independently determine the extent to which any medication caused these problems; however, I know that her condition was changing rapidly. Finally, Colistin was commenced intravenously. I was concerned about its potential effects on the kidneys and asked whether there was an opportunity to delay or reconsider the treatment while she recovered from some of the difficulties she had already developed. Nevertheless, the consultant proceeded with the treatment. I observed increasing fluid retention and swelling in my mother’s legs and feet. Her laboratory results showed significant abnormalities, including deterioration in her electrolytes. She became increasingly drowsy and semi-conscious. Eventually, her kidneys stopped producing urine. I cannot say from my own observations what ultimately caused her kidney failure or whether it could have been prevented. Those are questions for qualified independent medical experts reviewing her complete medical record. But I believe they are questions that deserve to be asked. Was her kidney function being monitored adequately? Were the risks and benefits of the medications being continually reassessed as her condition changed? Were there alternative treatment options? Was the deterioration recognised early enough? And when her condition began to deteriorate significantly, was escalation of care sufficiently prompt? The final hours Her breathing and blood pressure became increasingly unstable. There appeared to be a prolonged period during which doctors were conducting consultations, investigations and assessments. Eventually, a junior doctor on duty rushed her to the Intensive Care Unit and placed her in a glass-sided room. Within approximately 20 minutes, she died. I stood outside the glass enclosure watching her final moments. I asked to enter the room and hold her hand, but wasn’t allowed. Communication One of my serious concerns was not simply the treatment itself, but the way communication took place. I was particularly troubled because I felt that there was little opportunity for patients and carers to raise concerns or ask questions. On one occasion, I was told: “You are not helping your mother but causing problems.” There were occasions when I felt that asking questions was interpreted as challenging authority rather than as an attempt by a family member to participate appropriately in her care. I found it difficult to contact the consultant outside brief ward rounds, which is why I depended heavily on nurses to communicate my concerns. This created a serious barrier. When a patient’s condition is deteriorating, families should not feel afraid to speak. Nor should junior staff feel unable to raise concerns because they fear being reprimanded. A safe healthcare system should encourage questions, not silence them. The burden placed on the family At one point, the consultant instructed that my mother should receive two bags of blood. The junior doctors and nurses urgently asked me to arrange for it but it was not immediately available at the hospital’s blood bank and that I was expected to find a donor and organise the process. Repeated testing My mother underwent frequent blood tests while admitted. At times, blood was taken approximately every six hours, leaving her arms bruised. For many investigations, doctors issued vouchers that I had to take to the laboratory to pay for. On occasions, vouchers were delayed or could not be located, requiring me to pay for the tests again. The cost of investigations was substantial. On some days, the laboratory testing alone came to Rs25,000. Blood samples were sometimes collected at very late hours, including around 2am. I understand that critically ill patients require frequent monitoring and investigations but should the frequency, timing and necessity not be balanced against my mother’s age, physical condition, discomfort and overall clinical needs? Nursing care Some nurses were caring, knowledgeable and compassionate and I remain grateful to them. However, I also observed significant inconsistencies in nursing care. Initially, vital signs and urine output appeared to be monitored and recorded regularly. As time passed, I observed that documentation became less consistent. On one occasion, a nurse instructed me to record my mother’s urine output and monitor her vital signs. I was willing to help in any reasonable way, but I found it distressing to feel that responsibility for monitoring a critically ill patient was being transferred to a family member. At one stage, a nursing aide was shared across four wards. My mother sometimes had to wait for assistance to use the toilet or bedpan. For an elderly patient with serious burns and a deteriorating medical condition, these delays were deeply concerning. The pharmacy burden Another recurring problem was the responsibility placed on me to obtain medicines and equipment. Rather than receiving one comprehensive list of the items required for the day, I was sent to the pharmacy multiple times. I found myself running out to buy medicines, injections, syringes, dressings, fluids, drips and surgical masks—sometimes late at night. What needs to change I believe there are lessons that hospitals can and should take seriously. Compassion must be part of clinical care. Patients are human beings, not cases or diagnoses. Their families are often frightened and exhausted. They deserve kindness. Patients and carers should be treated with dignity and respect. Asking questions should not result in intimidation or dismissal. Patient-centred care must be genuine. Families who are closely involved in caring for an elderly or seriously ill patient may have valuable observations. Their concerns should be heard respectfully. Clinical decisions should be transparent. Patients and families should, where appropriate, receive understandable explanations about significant treatments, risks, alternatives and changes in condition. Hospitals need psychologically safe environments. Junior doctors, nurses and other healthcare workers must be able to raise concerns without fear of humiliation or retaliation. Clinical governance must be strong. When a patient’s condition deteriorates unexpectedly, there should be robust systems for reviewing what happened and identifying opportunities for improvement. Serious concerns deserve independent investigation. Families should not have to investigate a loved one’s final days on their own. Accountability should follow evidence. If an investigation identifies shortcomings in care, those shortcomings should be acknowledged, and meaningful steps should be taken to prevent them from happening again. Why I am speaking out I am speaking out because my mother was more than a patient number. She was an 83-year-old woman, a sister, a mother, and a grandmother. She deserved competent medical care, dignity, compassion and the opportunity to have her voice—and, when she could not speak for herself, her family’s observations—heard. I know that doctors and nurses work under enormous pressure. I know that some patients die despite excellent care. I know that hindsight can make complex medical decisions appear simpler than they were at the time. That is precisely why I am asking for an independent review rather than making definitive accusations. I want to know whether anything could reasonably have been done differently. If there were failures, I want those failures to be acknowledged and addressed. My mother cannot benefit from any changes that may result. But perhaps another elderly mother or another family, may. No family should leave a hospital carrying the unbearable uncertainty of wondering whether more could have been done for the person they loved. I am asking for transparency, accountability and, above all, better patient care.

items.title: Comment UnionPay connecte le monde grâce à ses services de paiement
items.description: Ge Mengchao, journaliste au Quotidien du Peuple À l'aéroport international de Shanghai Pudong, une touriste indonésienne nommée Nur est arrivée récemment avec sa fille, pour un voyage tant attendu en Chine. « Nous prévoyons de prendre le train à grande vitesse de Shanghai à Huangshan, dans la province de l'Anhui, puis de poursuivre notre voyage vers Jingdezhen et le mont Sanqingshan, dans la province du Jiangxi. Nous voulons voir et vivre un maximum d'expériences et nous immerger pleinement dans la beauté de la Chine », a-t-elle déclaré avec enthousiasme, ajoutant que « pour tout ce voyage, j'ai l'intention d'utiliser GoPay pour tous mes paiements, une chose impensable auparavant ». GoPay est un portefeuille électronique indonésien. Cette année, la Chine et l'Indonésie ont établi un accord d'interopérabilité transfrontalière pour les paiements par code QR. « Les utilisateurs chinois peuvent désormais utiliser des applications comme « Cloud QuickPass » (Yunshanfu) d'UnionPay pour effectuer des paiements en scannant des QR codes chez les commerçants indonésiens. Réciproquement, les utilisateurs indonésiens peuvent utiliser des portefeuilles électroniques comme GoPay pour régler instantanément leurs achats chez les commerçants chinois acceptant UnionPay ou Alipay », a expliqué un représentant d'UnionPay. UnionPay, une organisation internationale de cartes bancaires présente dans le monde entier, œuvre depuis des années à l'interconnexion des systèmes de paiement bilatéraux et multilatéraux au sein d'un réseau cohérent. En favorisant l'interopérabilité des systèmes d'acceptation des paiements, d'émission de cartes et de QR codes, UnionPay a bâti une infrastructure robuste capable de servir ses utilisateurs à travers le monde. Lors de leurs voyages en Asie du Sud-Est, notamment en Thaïlande et en Malaisie, les utilisateurs d'UnionPay peuvent régler leurs achats et leurs repas en scannant des QR codes avec leur portefeuille électronique compatible UnionPay. Au Moyen-Orient, par exemple aux Émirats arabes unis, les voyageurs peuvent effectuer des achats dans les aéroports ou les quartiers commerçants sans avoir besoin de changer de la monnaie locale. Et dans des pays africains comme l'Afrique du Sud, les cartes UnionPay peuvent être utilisées directement pour les séjours à l'hôtel et les dépenses quotidiennes, professionnelles ou personnelles. À ce jour, le réseau d'acceptation d'UnionPay s'étend à 183 pays et régions, couvrant plus de 100 millions de commerçants hors de la partie continentale de la Chine et connectant environ 2 600 institutions membres. Les cartes UnionPay sont émises dans 86 pays et régions à l'étranger, et l'entreprise a noué des partenariats avec des institutions internationales pour lancer plus de 200 portefeuilles numériques basés sur les normes UnionPay. Par ailleurs, UnionPay a amélioré l'interopérabilité des codes QR dans des pays comme l'Indonésie, la Corée du Sud, le Sri Lanka, l'Argentine et la Turquie, permettant ainsi à plus de 46 millions de commerçants à l'étranger d'accepter les paiements par code QR UnionPay. UnionPay demeure aussi pleinement engagé dans la transformation et le développement du secteur international des paiements. Ces dernières années, grâce à un modèle d'« intégration en un point unique », UnionPay a instauré une interopérabilité avec des réseaux de paiement par code QR dans divers pays et régions. L'entreprise a exporté ses systèmes de commutation et de compensation ainsi que ses normes techniques vers des pays comme le Laos et la Thaïlande ; elle a également pris part à l'élaboration de normes locales pour les paiements par code QR à Singapour et en Thaïlande, marquant ainsi un tournant stratégique : passer de la simple « construction de réseaux » à l'« établissement de règles ». « Prenons l'exemple de l'Asie du Sud : le secteur local des paiements y est encore à un stade embryonnaire. Les institutions sur place manquent souvent de capacités techniques internes solides, tandis que les prestataires de services externes imposent généralement des tarifs élevés et des cycles de développement longs. En tirant parti de notre plateforme d'émission de cartes basée sur le cloud, qui limite le besoin de refontes lourdes des systèmes existants, nous avons permis à trois institutions locales de commencer à émettre des cartes UnionPay », a expliqué un représentant d'UnionPay. « Proposer des solutions adaptées aux spécificités et aux défis rencontrés par les institutions locales est un principe fondamental pour une collaboration réussie », a-t-il ajouté. Par l'exportation de ses technologies et de ses normes, UnionPay a contribué à réduire les coûts de paiement dans plusieurs pays et régions participant à l'Initiative « La Ceinture et la Route », leur permettant ainsi de bénéficier des retombées des paiements numériques. Les services d'UnionPay ne se limitent pas à accompagner les utilisateurs et les entreprises chinoises dans leur développement à l'étranger ; ils sont désormais profondément intégrés au quotidien et aux activités professionnelles des habitants de nombreux pays et régions. Dans des pays comme les Émirats arabes unis, le Kenya, la Mongolie, Singapour, le Kazakhstan et le Bangladesh, les cartes UnionPay sont utilisées par les résidents locaux, notamment comme cartes de versement de salaire ou comme cartes d'étudiant faisant également office de moyen de paiement. Au Bangladesh, par exemple, des partenariats durables avec des institutions financières locales ont permis l'émission de millions de cartes UnionPay, faisant de l'organisation l'un des principaux émetteurs de cartes internationales dans le pays. « UnionPay » est devenue l'une des marques de « services chinois » les plus reconnues à l'étranger. Selon les projections du cabinet d'études de marché et d'analyse de données Nilson Report, UnionPay devrait se hisser, d'ici 2030, au premier rang mondial en termes de nombre de cartes en circulation. Soutenus par un réseau mondial en constante expansion, les services de paiement transfrontaliers de UnionPay gagnent en commodité. « UnionPay s’inscrit dans la stratégie d’ouverture de haut niveau de la Chine, en connectant le monde grâce à ses services de paiement et en agissant comme un pont financier entre la Chine et d’autres nations ; cela facilite aussi bien les flux de capitaux que les échanges entre les personnes », a ajouté le représentant de UnionPay.

items.title: Campagne non pluvieuse : L’opération « Un bas-fond, un forage » prend forme à Tibga
items.description: Dans le cadre du suivi du Plan d’urgence de la campagne non pluvieuse, le Ministre d’État, Ministre de l’Agriculture, de l’Eau, des Ressources animales et halieutiques, le camarade Commandant Ismaël SOMBIE, s’est rendu, ce mardi 10 novembre 2026, à Tibga, dans la région du Gulmu, pour s’assurer de l’effectivité des opérations de réalisation de forages sur le bas-fond rizicole de la commune, dans le cadre de l’opération « 𝐔𝐧 𝐛𝐚𝐬-𝐟𝐨𝐧𝐝, 𝐮𝐧 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 ». Cette initiative, conduite parallèlement à l’opération de réalisation de « 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐬 à 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐱 𝐬𝐮𝐛𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐧é » vise à renforcer durablement la maîtrise de l’eau et à offrir aux producteurs les moyens de développer une agriculture moins dépendante des aléas climatiques. Le choix du site de Tibga n’est pas fortuit. En septembre 2025, lors d’une précédente visite de suivi de la campagne agricole, le Camarade Ministre d’État avait parcouru ce bas-fond aménagé d’environ 40 hectares, exploité en majorité par des femmes. À cette occasion, les productrices avaient particulièrement attiré son attention sur les difficultés d’accès à l’eau, notamment pour assurer la production durant la saison sèche et faire face aux éventuelles poches de sécheresse. Face à cette préoccupation, le Ministre d’État avait annoncé des mesures visant à renforcer la disponibilité de l’eau sur le site. Un engagement qui se concrétise aujourd’hui à travers les travaux de forage entrepris dans le cadre du plan d’urgence de la campagne non pluvieuse. Sur le terrain, le constat est encourageant. Deux forages ont déjà été réalisés, avec des débits respectifs de 14 m³/heure et de 5 m³/heure. Ces ouvrages viennent renforcer les capacités d’approvisionnement en eau du bas-fond et offrir de nouvelles perspectives de production aux exploitants. À l’échelle nationale, l’opération « 𝐔𝐧 𝐛𝐚𝐬-𝐟𝐨𝐧𝐝, 𝐮𝐧 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 » prévoit la réalisation de 1 000 forages sur différents sites de production. L’ambition est de sécuriser l’accès à l’eau, de soutenir l’intensification des activités agricoles et de permettre aux producteurs de tirer pleinement profit du potentiel des aménagements hydroagricoles, indépendamment des saisons et des variations pluviométriques. Au cours des échanges avec les producteurs, le Camarade Ministre d’État les a encouragés à faire un usage responsable et optimal des infrastructures réalisées. Il les a notamment invités à diversifier leurs productions, en associant les cultures maraîchères aux céréales, afin de parvenir à trois cycles de production par an. « 𝑳’𝒐𝒃𝒋𝒆𝒄𝒕𝒊𝒇 𝒆𝒔𝒕 𝒅𝒆 𝒇𝒂𝒊𝒓𝒆 𝒅𝒆 𝒍’𝒆𝒂𝒖 𝒖𝒏 𝒗é𝒓𝒊𝒕𝒂𝒃𝒍𝒆 𝒍𝒆𝒗𝒊𝒆𝒓 𝒅𝒆 𝒑𝒓𝒐𝒅𝒖𝒄𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏, 𝒅𝒆 𝒄𝒓é𝒂𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏 𝒅𝒆 𝒓𝒊𝒄𝒉𝒆𝒔𝒔𝒆𝒔 𝒆𝒕 𝒅’𝒂𝒎é𝒍𝒊𝒐𝒓𝒂𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏 𝒅𝒆𝒔 𝒄𝒐𝒏𝒅𝒊𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏𝒔 𝒅𝒆 𝒗𝒊𝒆 𝒅𝒆𝒔 𝒑𝒐𝒑𝒖𝒍𝒂𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏𝒔 𝒓𝒖𝒓𝒂𝒍𝒆𝒔. », a-t-il souligné. À Tibga, la concrétisation de cet engagement illustre une orientation majeure du plan d’urgence : faire de la maîtrise de l’eau le socle d’une agriculture productive, résiliente et moins tributaire des caprices pluviométriques. Au-delà des ouvrages hydrauliques, c’est la capacité des producteurs à produire toute l’année, à accroître leurs revenus et à contribuer durablement à la souveraineté alimentaire qui est en jeu. items.title: Cameroun/Conseil constitutionnel : Remy Nama et Abdoulaye Daouda ont prêté serment
items.description: © DR Les deux nouveaux membres du Conseil constitutionnel ont sacrifié au rituel de prestation de serment ce 11 novembre 2026 au palais de Verre Paul Biya. Entre honneurs et rappel des responsabilités, le 7è congrès prend acte de leur engagement. La main gauche posée sur la Constitution, la main droite levée devant le drapeau tricolore, le nouveau président du Conseil constitutionnel Remy Nama et le nouveau membre dudit conseil, Abdoulaye Daouda ont pris tour à tour l’engagement : « Je jure de bien et fidèlement remplir mes fonctions, de les exercer en toute impartialité dans le respect de la Constitution, de garder le secret des délibérations, des votes, de ne prendre aucune position publique, de ne donner aucune consultation sur les questions relevant de la compétence du Conseil ». Par leur engagement, ils complètent la liste des 11 membres du Conseil constitutionnel. Laquelle manquaient deux personnalités à la suite du décès du président Clément Atangana et du membre Bah Oumarou Sanda. Les deux nouveaux membres ont prêté serment ce mercredi à l’hémicycle du Palais de Verre Paul Biya devant de nombreuses personnalités. Les députés et sénateurs, les responsables de la Cour suprême, les membres du Conseil constitutionnel, les membres du gouvernement, des représentants des missions diplomatiques, des représentants des organisations internationales et d’autres personnalités. Au cours de ce 7è congrès de l’histoire du Cameroun, le président de l’Assemblée nationale, président du Congrès, a félicité au nom du Congrès et à son nom personnel les deux personnalités à l’honneur. Le député Théodore Datouo a rappelé aux deux nouveaux membres du Conseil constitutionnel la responsabilité qui est la leur au-delà des honneurs qu'ils reçoivent : traiter des questions qui touchent au fondement des institutions, à la régularité démocratique et à la protection de l’ordre constitutionnel. Une mission qui exige une vigilance permanente, une stricte application des textes et une égale considération de tous les acteurs concernés. D’après lui, le serment lie les deux personnalités à la Constitution, à la République et aux exigences supérieur de leur charge Leur intégrité, leurs formations, leurs riches expériences tirées de leur parcours respectifs, leur compétence sont le gage qu’ils sont à la hauteur des responsabilités qui sont désormais les leurs. A court terme, ils sont déjà attendus sur la régularité du scrutin législatif du 07 février 2027 ainsi que sur la proclamation des résultats desdites élections. Cet article Cameroun/Conseil constitutionnel : Remy Nama et Abdoulaye Daouda ont prêté serment est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Boffa : Yick Fung Shipping poursuit son engagement en faveur de l’éducation
items.description: Le 3 novembre 2026, Yick Fung Shipping, en partenariat avec la Croix-Rouge Guinéenne, a organisé une cérémonie de donation de matériaux scolaires à l'école primaire de Soumbouyadi, dans la préfecture de Boffa, offrant à l'ensemble des élèves des manuels, des cartables et des kits de fournitures scolaires, tout en prévoyant de financer la rénovation des salles de classe de l'école afin d'améliorer davantage l'environnement d'enseignement. Cette initiative vise à soutenir le développement de l'éducation en Guinée, à améliorer les conditions d'apprentissage des élèves de l'école primaire de Soumbouyadi, à approfondir les relations de bon voisinage avec les communautés riveraines, à promouvoir la convergence sino-guinéenne et à assumer pleinement la responsabilité sociale de l'entreprise. Sur place, le président de la Croix-Rouge Guinéenne, des représentants des autorités locales, les responsables du secteur de l'éducation, les guides religieux et les autorités préfectorales se sont réunis, témoignant de l'importance accordée par toutes les parties à cette action citoyenne en faveur de l'éducation de base et du bien-être des communautés rurales. Pendant la cérémonie, les élèves ont présenté des prestations artistiques — chant, récitations et danses traditionnelles — exprimant ainsi leur joie et leur gratitude envers les donateurs ; de nombreux enseignants, élèves et parents d'élèves y ont également pris part et partagé cette joie Les dons remis comprennent 2285 manuels scolaires de la 1re à la 6e année, 797 sacs scolaires et 797 kits de fournitures scolaires; la société prévoit également de financer la rénovation des salles de classe de l'école. Ces fournitures couvrent l'ensemble des élèves du préscolaire et du primaire et améliorent non seulement les conditions d'apprentissage, mais favorisent aussi le développement global des élèves. M.Mangué Sylla, Directeur préfectoral de l'Éducation de Boffa, s'est félicité de la constance de cet accompagnement. Se réjouissant de cette nouvelle action sociale, il a rappelé que Yick Fung Shipping n'en était pas à son premier geste en faveur de l'école de Soumbouyadi : l'année précédente, au même endroit, l'entreprise avait déjà remis des kits scolaires et inauguré un forage aménagé. Selon lui, ce don témoigne de l'attention portée au système éducatif local et soutient utilement le travail des enseignants comme des apprenants. Au-delà de la dimension éducative, la cérémonie a également porté un message fort en faveur de la paix sociale et de la responsabilité communautaire. L'un des temps forts de la cérémonie a été l'intervention de M. Ding Yaming, Directeur général adjoint de COSCO SHIPPING. Son propos a pleinement illustré l'engagement social de l'entreprise : il a réaffirmé la volonté de la société d'accompagner durablement le développement des communautés riveraines, de faire progresser l'éducation locale et de soutenir le progrès socio-économique de la région, dans une logique de coopération, de respect mutuel et de bénéfice partagé : « Nous avons mené à plusieurs reprises des opérations de sauvetage en mer pour protéger la vie des pêcheurs de la localité ; nous continuons à faire don de bateaux de pêche, d'engins de pêche et de produits de première nécessité aux pêcheurs et aux habitants des environs, afin de les aider à vivre et à travailler en paix ; nous avons créé de nombreux emplois pour les populations de la région de Boffa, contribuant au développement des moyens d'existence locaux ; nous nous rendons régulièrement dans les écoles pour offrir des manuels et des produits d'hygiène, soutenant ainsi l'éducation de base.» «Comme on le dit souvent en Chine, les enfants sont l'avenir du pays et l'éducation est la lumière qui éclaire cet avenir. Ayant constaté que l'école primaire de Soumbouyadi disposait de conditions d'enseignement limitées, de matériel pédagogique insuffisant et d'infrastructures à améliorer, nous nous sommes immédiatement rapprochés de l'établissement et avons préparé cette action avec la plus grande sincérité, en rénovant des salles de classe et en faisant don de diverses fournitures scolaires. » Ce discours, sincère et empreint de considération, s'est poursuivi par un mot personnel : cette visite était aussi l'occasion de retrouver des collègues et des voisins, et de considérer chaque habitant de cette terre chaleureuse comme un membre de sa grande famille. M. Touré 1 Saloun, Gestionnaire des Ressources Humaines de la société, a déclaré que la présence d'une entreprise dans une localité ne doit pas se limiter à des activités économiques, mais doit aussi se traduire par des initiatives sociales propres à renforcer la confiance, le dialogue et la compréhension mutuelle. Il a souligné : « À travers ce don, nous souhaitons accompagner les élèves dans leur parcours scolaire, mais aussi consolider les relations entre notre société et les communautés. En retour, nous attendons une cohabitation pacifique, fondée sur le respect mutuel, le dialogue, la compréhension et la collaboration entre toutes les parties. Le développement durable ne peut se construire sans la paix et l'entente avec les communautés riveraines. ». Ce message rappelle une vérité fondamentale : aucune ambition de développement ne saurait prospérer durablement sans un climat de confiance, de respect réciproque et de coexistence harmonieuse entre les différents acteurs du territoire.À Soumbouyadi, l'action de Yick Fung Shipping prend ainsi tout son sens : rapprocher l'entreprise de son environnement humain, accompagner les aspirations éducatives et faire de la solidarité un instrument de cohésion sociale. Une entreprise qui soutient l'école participe à la formation des compétences de demain ; une entreprise qui accompagne les communautés contribue à renforcer le tissu social. À travers cette initiative, Yick Fung Shipping inscrit son action dans une dynamique où l'investissement économique trouve son prolongement dans l'humain, l'éducation et la paix sociale.

items.title: Réforme de l’administration : Le gouvernement veut mettre fin aux démarches papier
items.description: La dématérialisation des services publics au Maroc progresse, mais peine encore à transformer en profondeur les relations entre l’administration et les usagers. Le maintien de documents papier, le cloisonnement des systèmes d’information et les disparités entre les administrations continuent de freiner cette mutation. C’est le constat dressé mardi par Aïcha Guellaa, ministre déléguée auprès du ministre de l’Intelligence artificielle, de la Transition numérique et de la Réforme de l’administration, chargée de la Réforme de l’administration, devant la Chambre des conseillers. Lors de la séance hebdomadaire des questions orales, la responsable a plaidé pour un renforcement du dispositif législatif encadrant l’administration numérique, notamment à travers la reconnaissance de la valeur juridique des documents et des données échangés électroniquement entre les institutions publiques. Une évolution qu’elle considère comme indispensable pour dépasser les limites d’une numérisation encore trop souvent fragmentée. Pour Guellaa, la réussite de cette transformation ne saurait se mesurer au nombre de textes adoptés ou de plateformes lancées. Elle doit avant tout être appréciée à travers les changements concrets qu’elle apporte à la qualité des services publics et à leur accessibilité. Or, certaines initiatives législatives et institutionnelles tardent encore à produire des effets perceptibles dans les démarches des citoyens auprès de l’administration. Des progrès sont néanmoins enregistrés. La ministre déléguée a notamment cité la réduction du nombre de pièces administratives exigées pour constituer un dossier de retraite, passé de 11 documents à environ deux. Cette simplification résulte de la numérisation des procédures et du renforcement des échanges entre les différentes institutions concernées. L'enjeu consiste désormais à généraliser cette logique à l'ensemble des services publics. La numérisation et l'interconnexion des systèmes d'information doivent permettre de limiter les déplacements des usagers et de mettre fin à des pratiques qui persistent malgré les avancées technologiques. « Il n'est plus acceptable » de demander aux citoyens des documents déjà détenus par une autre administration, a souligné la responsable, estimant que les institutions publiques doivent assurer elles-mêmes la circulation de ces informations. Cette transformation dépasse, selon elle, le périmètre du département chargé de la réforme administrative. Elle constitue un projet national nécessitant l'implication des différents ministères, des institutions publiques, des établissements et entreprises publics ainsi que des collectivités territoriales. Le Parlement est également appelé à contribuer à cette dynamique à travers son travail législatif, ses missions de contrôle et la formulation de propositions. Sur le plan international, le Maroc a enregistré une progression dans le domaine de la numérisation administrative, passant de la 101e à la 51e place en 2024. Un résultat que Kellaâ attribue aux efforts engagés pour moderniser les services publics, tout en reconnaissant que ces avancées ne se traduisent pas encore de manière homogène dans les interactions quotidiennes des citoyens avec l'administration. L'ampleur de l'appareil administratif constitue, à cet égard, un facteur de complexité. Le dispositif concerne plus de 900.000 fonctionnaires répartis entre plus de 32 départements ministériels, 200 établissements et entreprises publics, 12 régions et plus de 1.500 communes. Il couvre également plus de 2.500 procédures administratives publiées sur le portail national « Idarati », ainsi que 874 services publics numériques de référence. Plusieurs dispositifs témoignent déjà de cette évolution. La ministre déléguée a notamment mentionné le Registre social, qui totalise plus de 20 millions d'inscriptions, la plateforme « Rokhas » consacrée aux demandes d'autorisation et le système « BADR » dédié aux déclarations douanières. Elle a également cité la carte nationale d'identité électronique et le passeport biométrique, dont le délai moyen de délivrance est de sept jours. À ces dispositifs s'ajoutent le programme d'aide au logement, dont les bénéficiaires peuvent effectuer les démarches sans fournir de documents ni se déplacer auprès de l'administration, ainsi que « PortNet », la plateforme dédiée aux procédures du commerce extérieur. Le portail national « Idarati » occupe également une place importante dans ce processus. Plus de 2.533 décisions administratives concernant plus de 120 administrations publiques y sont publiées. Les usagers peuvent ainsi consulter en amont les pièces à fournir, les étapes de traitement de leurs dossiers, les délais prévus et les administrations compétentes. Le dispositif vise à rendre les procédures plus lisibles et à améliorer la transparence des relations entre l'administration et les citoyens. Mais la multiplication des outils numériques ne suffit pas à garantir une véritable dématérialisation. Dans de nombreux cas, les services continuent de fonctionner de manière indépendante, selon les systèmes propres à chaque administration. Les parcours hybrides, associant démarches en ligne et documents papier, restent fréquents, tandis que les plateformes communes ne sont pas encore suffisamment généralisées. Certaines dispositions réglementaires sectorielles imposent par ailleurs toujours la présence physique des usagers ou la présentation de dossiers sous format papier. C'est précisément sur ces blocages que le gouvernement entend intervenir. Aïcha Guellaa a annoncé la préparation d'un nouveau texte législatif destiné à reconnaître la valeur juridique et probante des données échangées par voie électronique entre les administrations. Le projet prévoit également de substituer à l'obligation de présence physique un système de compte numérique permettant de vérifier l'identité des usagers tout en assurant la protection de leurs données personnelles. Le département travaille, dans ce cadre, à l'élaboration d'un texte qui sera soumis au Parlement afin de définir les modalités d'identification numérique des usagers, notamment à partir de leur numéro de téléphone ou de leur photographie. L'ambition est de mettre en place un dispositif unifié permettant aux citoyens d'interagir avec les différentes administrations, à l'instar de certaines expériences internationales. La responsable a également identifié plusieurs difficultés qui continuent de ralentir le chantier : la progression insuffisamment rapide de la numérisation des procédures, la persistance des démarches papier, le manque d'interconnexion entre les administrations et les écarts de maturité numérique entre les institutions. À ces contraintes s'ajoutent les enjeux liés à l'accompagnement du changement et à la garantie d'un accès équitable et sécurisé aux services publics. Pour la prochaine étape, le programme d'action du ministère s'organisera autour de six axes. Il prévoit le renforcement de la gouvernance, du suivi et de l'évaluation ; l'accompagnement de la transformation numérique de l'administration et l'accélération de la simplification des procédures et de la dématérialisation des parcours administratifs ; le développement du portail national « Idarati » ; le parachèvement du cadre juridique et réglementaire de l'administration numérique ; l'organisation des données et le développement de systèmes numériques communs ; enfin, l'amélioration de l'accueil, la facilitation de l'accès aux services et la mesure de leurs effets sur les usagers. Au-delà des plateformes et des outils déployés, le principal défi reste ainsi de faire de la numérisation un changement concret dans le fonctionnement des services publics, en réduisant les démarches imposées aux citoyens et en faisant de l'échange de données entre administrations une pratique systématique. The post Réforme de l’administration : Le gouvernement veut mettre fin aux démarches papier appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Barcelona se queda sin metro más de 10 horas durante la huelga general
items.description: La huelga general de este miércoles deja a Cataluña durante 10 horas y 30 minutos sin servicio de transporte público tanto ferroviario como por carretera. Desde las 9.30 de la mañana y hasta las 16.30 de la tarde, Rodalies, Ferrocarrils de la Generalitat de Catalunya (FGC), el metro de Barcelona y los autobuses urbanos e interurbanos han suspendido las circulaciones de acuerdo con los servicios mínimos establecidos por la Generalitat. Tampoco prestarán servicio de las 21.00 hasta la medianoche . En las horas punta -de 6.30 a 9.30 y de 16.30 a 21.00- solo circularán el 25% de los trenes y autobuses habituales. Los servicios mínimos los ha fijado la Generalitat y son inferiores a los de las últimas huelgas generales de 2012 cuando en hora punta se garantizó el 33%. La jornada también ha provocado importantes problemas de movilidad por los cortes de carreteras y la cancelación de 85 vuelos -de los 734 programados- en el aeropuerto de Barcelona-El Prat.
